• Assembling the transformer architecture
Tracing the origins of the transformer model
Models represented by RNNs and LSTMs perform excellently in handling sequential data. However,
due to their serial computing characteristics, they are inefficient during training and inference.
The fundamental reason lies in the processing logic of RNN and LSTM models, where the output
at each time step depends not only on the current input but also on the output of the previous time
step. This means that the output for all previous time steps must be computed before calculating
the output at the current time step.
Moreover, RNN models struggle with long-distance dependencies, as issues such as vanishing
or exploding gradients make it difficult for the model to learn such dependencies. LSTM models
alleviate the problems of vanishing or exploding gradients by introducing memory gate
mechanisms, enabling them to handle long-distance dependencies more effectively.
To address this issue, the Google AI team proposed the Transformer model in 2017, a deep learning
model designed for processing sequential data. The introduction of the Transformer marked a
shift in the field of natural language processing from traditional models such as RNN, LSTM, and
GRU to a new era of deep learning models capable of parallel training. Currently, the most popular
large language models are all built based on the Transformer model. Therefore, understanding
the basic principles of the Transformer model is crucial for mastering the working mechanisms
and application scenarios of large language models. To understand why the Transformer became
the foundation of modern large language models, it is useful to look next at the core principles of
its architecture: how it represents input sequences, how attention captures relationships between
tokens, and how the encoder and decoder work together to process language.
Understanding the core principles of the transformer
architecture
The paper Attention is All You Need is the pioneering work of the Transformer model, proposing
a brand-new sequence modeling method—the Self-Attention Mechanism. Self-attention is a
technique used to capture dependencies within input sequences, allowing the establishment of
long-range dependencies between different positions. Its core lies in calculating a weight for each
position in the input sequence, reflecting the dependency of that position with other positions.

Chapter 2 21
This mechanism enables the model to capture long-range dependencies between different
positions, thereby better handling dependencies in sequential data. The architecture of the model
is shown in Figure 2.1.
Figure 2.1: Architecture of the Transformer model
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 22
The Transformer model consists of an encoder and a decoder. The encoder is made up of
multiple stacked identical layers, each including a Multi-Head Attention Mechanism and a
Feed-Forward Neural Network. The decoder is also composed of multiple stacked identical
layers, each comprising a multi-head attention mechanism, a feed-forward neural network, and
an encoder-decoder attention mechanism. The encoder and decoder are connected via residual
connections and layer normalization. This structural design of the model can effectively capture
dependencies within the input sequence, thus enhancing the expressive power of the model.
To understand how this architecture works in practice, it is useful to break the Transformer into
the main components that process input tokens, preserve sequence order, calculate contextual
relationships, and stabilize training. The success of the Transformer model relies on the following
seven key technological innovations.
Word embedding
Word embedding is one of the core technologies of the Transformer model, capable of transforming
each word in the input sequence into a vector to represent the semantic information of that word.
The core idea of word embedding is that the model generates a vector for each word in the input
sequence, and these vectors are combined to represent the semantic information of the input
sequence. The design of word embedding allows the model to better capture the semantic features
in the input sequence, thereby improving the model’s expressive power.
Positional encoding
Since the Transformer model does not contain any recurrent relationships associated with
position, it requires a method to represent the positional information within the input sequence.
Positional Encoding is a technique used to represent the position information in the input
sequence, capable of generating a position vector for each position in the sequence to express its
positional information. Positional encoding is an indispensable component of the Transformer
model, compensating for its lack of a recursive structure.
Self-attention mechanism
The self-attention mechanism is the core of the Transformer model. Its core idea is that for
each position in the input sequence, the model calculates a weight to represent the dependency
relationship between this position and other positions. This mechanism enables the model to
capture long-range dependencies between different positions, thus better understanding the

51972.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51972.heading: Chapter 2 23
51972.content:
Chapter 2 23
Multi-head attention mechanism
The multi-head attention mechanism is an extension of the self-attention mechanism, capable
of capturing dependencies in the input sequence more effectively. Its core idea is that the model
computes multiple different self-attention scores and merges these scores to represent the
dependencies between different positions in the input sequence. The robustness and scalability
of the multi-head attention mechanism enhance the stability of the model and make it extensible
to other types of attention mechanisms.
Feedforward neural network
The feedforward neural network is another core component of the Transformer model, capable
of performing nonlinear transformations on each position of the input sequence. The core idea of
the feedforward neural network is to perform nonlinear transformations on each position of the
input sequence and integrate these transformation results to represent the feature information
of the input sequence. The flexibility of the feedforward neural network allows it to be combined
with other types of network layers to achieve more complex functions.
Residual connection
Residual connection is one of the core designs in the Transformer model and can improve the
training efficiency of the model. Its core idea is that the model adds the input and output of each
position in the input sequence, and uses the result as the input to the next layer. This design
enables the model to better capture the feature information in the input sequence, thereby
enhancing training efficiency.
Layer normalization
Layer normalization is one of the core techniques in the Transformer model and can improve the
training efficiency of the model. Its core idea is that the model normalizes each position in the
input sequence and uses the normalized result as the input to the next layer. This design is widely
used in various sub-layers of both the encoder and decoder to enhance the model’s capability of
handling sequences of different lengths and its generalization performance.
To understand how this architecture works in practice, it is useful to break the Transformer into
the main components that process input tokens, preserve sequence order, calculate contextual
relationships, and stabilize training.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 24
Representing text with word embeddings
Neural networks cannot process raw text directly, so text must first be converted into numerical
representations. Word embeddings provide a way to represent words as dense vectors that can
capture semantic relationships between them. This section first explains why simple encoding
methods such as one-hot encoding are limited, then shows how word embeddings can be learned
through a small neural network example and visualized in a two-dimensional space.

51973.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51973.heading: Chapter 2 23
51973.content:
Before examining how word embeddings learn semantic relationships, it is useful to begin with
the simplest question: how can words be represented as numbers at all?
Converting text into numerical representations
One simple method is to use One-Hot encoding. One-Hot encoding is a technique that converts
text data into numerical data, enabling each word in the input sequence to be transformed into a
vector to represent its semantics. The core idea of One-Hot encoding is that the model generates
a vector for each word in the input sequence and then combines these vectors to represent the
semantics of the input sequence.
We can explain the principle of One-Hot encoding with an example. Suppose we have a vocabulary
where each word has a number, and each word can be represented by a vector in which each
dimension corresponds to a word, as shown in Figure 2.2.
Figure 2.2: Example of the concept of converting text to an encoded representation
This method has some limitations in that it cannot effectively capture the semantic relationships
between words, as it only processes words independently and does not consider similarities
between words.

51974.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51974.heading: Chapter 2 25
51974.content:
Chapter 2 25
To address this problem, we can use word embedding techniques. Words with similar meanings
are closer in the word embedding space, while words with different meanings are farther apart.
Word embedding technology maps each word into a continuous vector space so that the semantic
relationships between words can be captured more accurately. For example, words with similar
meanings are closer together in the word embedding space, while words with dissimilar meanings
are farther apart. Suppose we have a simple text corpus containing only the following content:
I like raising dogs.
He likes raising cats.
He likes planting trees.
After preprocessing the text, the vocabulary obtained is: “I” “like” “raising” “dogs” “he” “cats”
“planting” “trees.” We can use word embedding techniques to convert these words into vectors
and visualize these vectors in a two-dimensional space, as shown in Figure 2.3.
Figure 2.3: Schematic diagram of word embedding mapped to 2D space
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 26
Although one-hot encoding can represent words numerically, it treats each word as independent
and cannot capture similarity between words. Word embeddings address this limitation by
learning dense vector representations in which related words can appear closer together in vector
space.
How do word embeddings achieve this effect
We can regard word embedding as a learning task, constructing a probabilistic prediction model
for words using neural network models. To see how this works in practice, the following example
builds a small word embedding model from a simple English corpus. The first step is to prepare
the environment, create the sample dataset, build the vocabulary, and convert word pairs into
training examples.
Environment preparation and data initialization
The following code demonstrates the basic data processing flow for word embeddings:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import random
import numpy as np
# Set random seed
def set_seed(seed_value=42):
torch.manual_seed(seed_value)
torch.cuda.manual_seed(seed_value)
torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed_value) # If using multiple GPUs
torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True
torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
np.random.seed(seed_value)
random.seed(seed_value)
set_seed(42) # Call the function and set the seed
# Create a dataset from sentences
raw_text_list = [
'I like cats',
'he likes dogs',

51975.heading: Chapter 2 27
51975.content:
Chapter 2 27
'he plants trees'
]
# Split sentences into word groups
word_list = [sentence.split() for sentence in raw_text_list]
# Flatten the word list into one large list
raw_text = [word for sentence in word_list for word in sentence]
vocab = set(raw_text)
vocab_size = len(vocab)
word_to_ix = {word: i for i, word in enumerate(vocab)}
ix_to_word = {i: word for i, word in enumerate(vocab)}
# Create data pairs, each containing the current word and the next word
data = []
for sentence in word_list:
for i in range(len(sentence) - 1):
context = sentence[i]
target = sentence[i + 1]
data.append((context, target))
The above code covers the following aspects:
• Data Processing: The raw text is split into words and converted into a series of (current
word, next word) pairs. These pairs serve as the model’s input and output (target), and
are used to analyze the probability distribution of each word and the next word during
model training.
• Vocabulary: All unique words form a vocabulary; each word is assigned a unique index.
• Random Seed: Set the random seed to ensure reproducibility of the results. This is
important because in deep learning, setting the random seed guarantees that the model’s
training results are reproducible. However, since our dataset is too simple and may be
affected by different programming system environments, you may get different results
during actual testing.
After the dataset and vocabulary have been prepared, the next step is to define the neural network
that will learn the word embeddings. The model begins with an embedding layer, then uses linear
layers and an activation function to predict the next word from the current word.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 28
Model definition
• Embedding Layer: The first layer of the model converts word indices into dense vectors
of fixed size. These vectors are learnable and will be updated during training to better
capture the semantic relationships between words.
• Linear Layers and Activation Function: The embedding vectors pass through two linear
layers and a ReLU activation function in sequence, forming the model’s hidden layers to
enhance the model’s nonlinear expressive capability.
• Output Layer: The final linear layer maps the output of the hidden layers to a vector
with the same size as the vocabulary. This vector is transformed into a probability
distribution using the log_softmax function, representing the probability of each word
in the vocabulary being the next word, given the current word.
class Model(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, vocab_size, embed_size):
super(Model, self).__init__()
self.embeddings = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_size)
self.linear1 = nn.Linear(embed_size, 128)
self.linear2 = nn.Linear(128, 64)
self.linear3 = nn.Linear(64, vocab_size)

self.activation = nn.ReLU()
def forward(self, inputs):
embeds = self.embeddings(inputs)
out = self.activation(self.linear1(embeds))
out = self.activation(self.linear2(out))
out = self.linear3(out)
log_probs = nn.functional.log_softmax(out, dim=1)
return log_probs

Once the model structure has been defined, it can be trained on the word-pair data. During training,
the model compares its predicted next-word distribution with the actual next word, calculates
the loss, and updates the embedding vectors through backpropagation.

51978.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51978.heading: Chapter 2 29
51978.content:
Chapter 2 29
Training process
For each (current word, next word) pair, the current word’s index is used as input, and the model’s
forward pass generates the probability distribution of the next word. Using the negative log
likelihood loss function (NLLLoss), the model’s predictions are compared with the actual next
word to calculate the loss value. Through backpropagation and gradient descent (using the SGD
optimizer), model parameters (including embedding vectors) are adjusted to reduce the loss.
# Create model
model = Model(vocab_size, EMBEDDING_DIM)
loss_function = nn.NLLLoss()
optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)
# Train model
for epoch in range(3000):
total_loss = 0
for context, target in data:
context_idx = torch.tensor([word_to_ix[context]], dtype=torch.
long)
model.zero_grad()
log_probs = model(context_idx)
loss = loss_function(log_probs, torch.tensor([word_to_ix[target]],
dtype=torch.long))
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
total_loss += loss.item()
if epoch % 50 == 0: # Print the loss value once every 50 epochs
print(f'Epoch {epoch}, Loss: {total_loss}')
After training, the learned embedding vectors can be inspected visually. Plotting the vectors in
two-dimensional space helps show whether the model has learned useful relationships between
words in the small training corpus.
Visualization of word embeddings
After training is completed, extract the embedding vector for each word and visualize them in
a two-dimensional space. The positions of these embedding vectors in space should reflect the
semantic relationships between words, such as similar words being mapped to locations close
to each other.

# Get word embeddings and plot
embeddings = model.embeddings.weight.data.numpy()
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))
for i, word in ix_to_word.items():
plt.scatter(embeddings[i][0], embeddings[i][1])
plt.annotate(
word,
xy=(embeddings[i][0], embeddings[i][1]),
xytext=(5, 2),

The above code is primarily used to illustrate the main workflow of designing and training a
word embedding model. It demonstrates the fundamental principles and training process of
word embedding models from an experimental perspective. In practical applications, the training
process for word embedding models is more complex. For example, there are multiple details in
this example that can be further optimized:
• Data Preprocessing Stage: The data preprocessing stage ignores issues such as how
to handle stop words and punctuation. Tokenization for large blocks of text is not
demonstrated.
• Model Training Process: In the model training process, this example passes the index
of a single word (via context_idx). However, when dealing with natural language

processing tasks, especially when using embedding layers, it is common to process a
batch of data rather than a single data point. This approach can improve training efficiency
and is also the data processing method expected by most deep learning frameworks. For
demonstration purposes, the example handles a single data point, but this is not best

The model training process uses a simple SGD optimizer. In practical applications, more

51980.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51980.heading: Chapter 2 31
51980.content:
Chapter 2 31
Typically, the training process also includes a validation step for evaluating the model’s
performance on unseen data, thereby monitoring and preventing overfitting. This part
is not covered in this example.
Word embeddings allow the Transformer model to represent the meaning of tokens as numerical
vectors, but they do not by themselves tell the model where each token appears in a sequence.
Since word order is essential for understanding language, the next section introduces positional
encoding, which adds sequence-position information to the token representations.
Encoding word order with positional information
Positional encoding is a key design in the Transformer model that allows it to process sequence
order without relying on recurrence or convolution. Without positional information, the
Transformer would treat the input as a set of tokens and would not be able to distinguish where
each token appears in a sentence. This could cause the model to misunderstand sentences where
word order changes the meaning, such as “He fights the tiger” and “The tiger fights him.”
Positional encoding addresses this problem by adding position information to the token
embeddings before they are processed by the self-attention mechanism. As a result, the model
can use both the meaning of each token and its position in the sequence when learning sentence
structure and context.
The original Transformer paper, Attention Is All You Need, used sinusoidal positional encoding. In
this approach, the encoding for each position is generated using sine and cosine functions. For
each position in the sequence, the positional encoding is defined as follows:
For even dimensions 2i:
PE(pos, 2i) = sin(wi × pos)
For odd dimensions 2i + 1:
PE(pos, 2i + 1) = cos(wi × pos)
Here, 𝑤𝑤𝑖𝑖  is a frequency parameter related to dimension 𝑖𝑖 , usually set as 𝑤𝑤𝑖𝑖 = 1/10000
2𝑖𝑖 / 𝑖𝑖 model ,
where 𝑑𝑑 model  represents the model dimension.
The main advantage of sinusoidal positional encoding is that it can represent relative position
relationships through linear transformations. Because the encoding is generated from fixed
mathematical functions rather than learned for a fixed maximum sequence length, it can be
applied to sequences of different lengths. However, for very long sequences, the periodic nature
of sine and cosine functions may make distant positions harder to distinguish, which can affect
the model’s ability to capture subtle long-range positional relationships.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 32
Later models, such as BERT and GPT-2, used learned absolute positional embeddings. In this
approach, each position has a learned vector that is added to the token embedding. For example,
BERT uses the sum of token embeddings, segment embeddings, and positional embeddings as

51981.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51981.heading: Chapter 2 31
51981.content:
its input representation, as shown in Figure 2.4.
Figure 2.4: The concept of absolute positional encoding in the BERT model
Learned absolute positional embeddings are straightforward to implement because each position
is assigned a trainable vector. However, they are usually tied to a predefined maximum sequence
length. For example, BERT is commonly configured with a maximum input length of 512 tokens.
If a sequence exceeds the supported length, the model cannot directly use learned positional
embeddings for the additional positions unless the architecture or embedding table is extended.
To address the limitations of fixed or absolute position representations, researchers have proposed
relative positional encoding methods. Instead of representing only the absolute position of each
token, these methods model the relative distance between tokens. One influential approach is
relation-aware self-attention, where relative position representations are incorporated into the
attention calculation so that the model can account for how far apart tokens are from one another.
The core advantage of relative position encoding lies in its ability to capture the relative positional
relationships between elements in a sequence through learned positional representations. This
allows the model to better understand and distinguish the relative distances and directions
between different positions. A major drawback of relative position encoding is that it depends
on specific task data, so it may not generalize well to other tasks. In addition, the computational
cost of relative position encoding can be high, as it requires calculating the relative position
between every pair of elements. This may decrease the efficiency of model training and inference.
Building on the idea of relative position information, newer techniques such as Rotary Position
Embedding (RoPE) and Attention with Linear Biases (ALiBi) have been introduced. RoPE
incorporates relative position information through rotation operations applied during attention
computation, making it effective for handling longer sequences without adding many extra
parameters. Models in the Llama family and Falcon use RoPE.

51982.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51982.heading: Chapter 2 33
51982.content:
Chapter 2 33
ALiBi introduces a linear bias into the attention scores so that the model can account for relative
distance during attention calculation. Instead of adding a separate positional embedding to the
token representation, ALiBi modifies the attention scores directly. This helps the model handle
longer contexts more efficiently and allows positional information to influence attention behavior.
Because RoPE and ALiBi modify how positional information is incorporated into attention, they
will be revisited in the next section when the self-attention mechanism is introduced.
Overall, positional encoding methods have evolved from fixed sinusoidal encodings to learned
absolute embeddings and relative-position techniques such as RoPE and ALiBi. These developments
have improved Transformer models in several ways:
• Generalization: Positional encoding methods help models handle sequences of different
lengths more effectively
• Flexibility: Learned or relative position representations allow models to adapt positional
information to specific tasks and architectures
• Efficiency: Relative-position methods such as RoPE and ALiBi can improve long-sequence
processing by incorporating position information directly into attention computation
• Performance: Better positional representations help models capture long-distance
dependencies and improve performance across NLP tasks
Positional information tells the Transformer where each token appears in a sequence, but position
alone is not enough for understanding language. The model must also determine which tokens
are most relevant to one another in a given context. The next section introduces the attention
mechanism, which allows the Transformer to calculate these relationships and assign greater
importance to the parts of the sequence that matter most for the current prediction.
Explaining the attention mechanism
The attention mechanism is an extremely sophisticated data processing technique. It enables
the model, when dealing with a sequence, to not only focus on different positions within the
sequence but also on the relationships between elements inside the sequence. Self-attention is
an extension of the attention mechanism; it provides a more flexible and powerful way to handle
sequential data, allowing the model to establish direct dependencies between any positions in
a sequence. The introduction of the self-attention mechanism, especially in the Transformer
model, has become a milestone in the NLP field, greatly advancing the development of pretrained
language models.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 34
Below, we will explain the core elements of the self-attention mechanism through a simple
example and then briefly introduce its implementation in the Transformer model.

51983.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51983.heading: Chapter 2 33
51983.content:
Suppose you encounter the following fill-in-the-blank question, as shown in Figure 2.5, which is
a typical conceptual diagram of the attention mechanism.
Buy apples or buy ______
Figure 2.5: Conceptual diagram of the attention mechanism for “apples”
If there is no further context, it is difficult to determine what should be filled in the blank. However,
if the context is that the fruit at home has been eaten up, you can infer that the blank should
be filled with another kind of fruit, such as “oranges.” If the context is that your wife’s phone is
broken, then you can infer that the blank should be filled with Samsung or Xiaomi, because in
this case, “apple” refers to a phone.

51984.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51984.heading: Chapter 2 35
51984.content:
Chapter 2 35
Through the demonstration in Figure 2.5, we can understand attention as the association
relationship between keywords and context. Suppose the attention mechanism connects the
blank with mobile phones, then the content to fill in becomes a matter of choosing between
different phone brands. If the attention mechanism links the blank with fruits, then the filled
content is a matter of choosing between different fruits. The probabilities of different brands or
fruits appearing are related to the sample data provided during training.
The attention mechanism first appeared in the paper Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning
to Align and Translate. This paper proposed a new neural machine translation model that combines
the encoder-decoder architecture with the attention mechanism, enabling the model to focus
on the parts of the input sequence most relevant to the current output. The initially introduced
attention mechanism was mainly used to weight the outputs of the encoder so that the decoder
could focus on the parts of the input sequence most relevant to the current generated word. This
mechanism is generally used as a component of the encoder-decoder architecture.
The attention mechanism in the paper Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align
and Translate is divided into two parts: learning global correspondences and learning local
correspondences.
Learning global correspondences
The model uses a single attention mechanism to learn the global correspondences between the
source and target languages. Specifically, the model first encodes each word in the source and
target languages using word embeddings to obtain word vectors. Then, the attention mechanism
is used to compute the similarity between each target word and all source words. Finally, a
weighted sum based on attention weights is performed on the source words to obtain a context
vector relevant to the target word.
Learning local correspondences
The model first uses the context vector from the first stage as a query vector, then uses the
source language word vectors as key vectors and value vectors, and finally calculates the local
correspondences between each target word and all source words through the attention mechanism.
The attention mechanism was first used to help a decoder focus on relevant parts of an encoded
source sequence. In the Transformer model, this idea is extended through self-attention, where
the words within the same sequence compare with one another to determine which tokens are
most relevant in context.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 36
Showing how self-attention captures sentence context
The basic principle of the self-attention mechanism is the comparison of similarity between
words. In the attention mechanism, every word is compared for similarity with other words,

51985.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51985.heading: Chapter 2 35
51985.content:
and the degree of similarity determines the importance of each word within the sentence. This
similarity comparison helps the model better understand semantic relationships in the sentence,
and thus more accurately capture the semantic information of the sentence.
Its specific principle can be explained in three parts: word embedding transformation, similarity
calculation, and spatial transformation.
Word embedding transformation
Converting textual information into vector representations is necessary for computers to
understand text, since computers can only process numeric information. A good word embedding
model enables computers to better comprehend the text and thus capture its semantic information
more effectively.
Similarity calculation
Calculate the similarity between each word in a sentence and every other word. This step is aimed
at finding the correlation between each word and every other word in the sentence.
Spatial transformation
Apply different transformations to the word embedding vector data to find the most suitable
transformation method, so as to better capture the semantic relationships between words.
Next, let’s use a simple example to illustrate this process. Suppose the following sentence is input:
My wife's phone is broken, should I buy an Apple or Android?
First, the computer will extract the words from the text and convert them into vector representations.
High-quality word embedding models can help computers better understand text and thus
capture semantic information more accurately. We use the pre-trained model bert-base-uncased
and reduce the word embeddings to two dimensions using PCA, thereby visualizing the words
in these two sentences. Figure 2.6 shows the visualization effect of the word embedding vectors.

51986.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51986.heading: Chapter 2 37
51986.content:
Chapter 2 37
Figure 2.6: Visualization of word embedding vectors in 2D space
When processing sequences (such as text), the attention mechanism allows the model to
dynamically focus on certain parts of the sequence. This mechanism enables the model to
identify and assign higher weights to keywords in a sentence, thereby improving the efficiency
and effectiveness of information processing. The processing flow is roughly divided into the
following four steps:
1. Similarity calculation � The model calculates the similarity between each word in the
sentence (called the “query”) and all other words (called the “keys”), usually achieved
via dot product or other correlation measures.
2. Normalization � Next, the softmax function is used to normalize these similarity scores,
so that the sum of all scores corresponding to each word equals 1. The purpose of this
step is to convert the raw similarity scores into a probability distribution, highlighting
the words in the sentence that are most relevant to the current word.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 38
3. Weighted sum � After normalized scoring for each word, the model computes a weighted
sum of the “values” of all words in the sentence to generate a weighted representation.
This step focuses on the parts most relevant to the current word, reducing or ignoring
the influence of less relevant parts.
4. Output � Finally, the model generates a weighted representation for each word in the
sentence, capturing the interrelations between words and their relative importance to
the current word.
We performed similarity calculation on the above word embedding vectors, and the results of
the similarity calculation between words are shown in Figure 2.7.
Figure 2.7: Similarity calculation results

51987.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51987.heading: Chapter 2 39
51987.content:
Chapter 2 39
Through softmax normalization, we can obtain the weights of each word relative to other words.
By computing the “weighted sum,”, we realize an attention-based update of word correlations. A
comparison between word embedding and attention weight embedding is shown in Figure 2.8.
Figure 2.8: Comparison of word embeddings and attention weight embeddings
The left side of Figure 2.8 shows the output of the original word embedding model, while the
right side presents the weights computed through the attention mechanism. By comparison, we
can observe three changes after adding attention weights:
• The position of “one phone broke” is tighter, making the grouping with other phrases
more distinct
• The relationship between the words “buy” and “Android” is closer
• The positional relationship between “Android” and “Apple” is closer, which can be judged
by the value changes on the vertical axis
The above case is merely a simple simulation of attention weight calculation. In fact, within the
Transformer model, the attention mechanism is implemented through Multi-Head Attention.
Multi-head attention allows the model to focus on different parts of the input sequence
simultaneously, thereby improving the model’s expressiveness and generalization ability.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 40
This conceptual example shows why attention is useful: it allows the model to assign different
levels of importance to different tokens based on context. The next section moves from this
intuition to implementation by explaining how Transformer self-attention uses query, key, and
value representations to calculate attention weights in practice.
Implementing transformer self-attention
In the previous sections, the attention mechanism of the Transformer model was explained
from a conceptual and theoretical perspective. However, the actual design and implementation
of the model are more complex. This section will explain the practical workflow of the attention
mechanism and the multi-head attention mechanism.
The attention mechanism addresses the following two problems.
It enables dynamic focus on the information most relevant to the current task, regardless of the
position of that information in the sequence. This is not limited to relationships within a sentence
but also includes long-range dependencies across sentences and even entire documents.
The attention mechanism dynamically assigns weights to each word in a sequence, allowing for
more effective use of long-distance contextual information and thus improving the accuracy of
the next word prediction.
The data processing workflow of the Transformer model includes the following four steps:
1. At the input stage, the Transformer model converts text sequences into word embedding

51988.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51988.heading: Chapter 2 39
51988.content:
vectors, and supplements positional encoding information in the word embedding vectors
(using sine and cosine encoding, respectively, for odd and even positions)
2. Using word embeddings containing positional encoding information, the model generates
corresponding query (Q), key (K), and value (V) representations through the Q, K, and
V weight matrices in the model. These representations are used to calculate attention
weights, which reflect the correlation among different parts of the input sequence. By
combining the computed attention weights with the values, the final attention output is
generated. This output captures the contextual information of the sequence and can be
used for the next layer of the model.
3. After the processing of each Transformer layer, the result calculated by the attention
mechanism is directly added into the residual network. The data then passes through the
feed-forward network, goes through the residual connection and layer normalization, and
is finally normalized to yield the probability distribution for the next word prediction result.

51989.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51989.heading: Chapter 2 41
51989.content:
Chapter 2 41
4. The predicted result is used as new input, and together with previous inputs, positional
encoding is updated for further prediction processing. In this process, multi-head masked
processing is involved. To ensure that the model does not “see” words that have not
yet been predicted during training, a mask is used to cover these words, simulating the
generation process during inference and ensuring that each prediction is made based
only on preceding words.
The implementation of positional encoding has been explained earlier. This section focuses on
how to train and learn with word embedding vectors containing positional encoding information.
First, we start with the calculation of word similarity. The core of the attention mechanism is to
identify important information in a sentence, with these important associations obtained through
word similarity calculations. The result of the similarity calculation is highly dependent on the
word embedding model. In natural language processing, the same word may have completely
different meanings in different contexts. To enable the model to accurately judge the similarity
of words based on context and determine their meanings in specific scenarios, we need to train
auxiliary model parameters to dynamically adjust weights according to the context, construct
updated word embedding vectors, allow the model to capture subtle differences in context,
and assign different interpretations to the same words while preserving the original semantic
information.
Let’s illustrate this process with a simple example.
Suppose during training, the Transformer is given the input sentence: “one Apple phone.” The
attention mechanism of the Transformer model will compare the similarity of each word in the
sentence with other words and determine the importance of each word in the sentence based
on the similarity scores. Taking the similarity calculation between “Apple” and “phone” as an
example, we can show the necessity of training the Q and K weight matrices.
As mentioned earlier, in the simulated two-dimensional word vector space, “Apple” could be
related both to “fruit” and to “phone.” The raw word embedding vectors cannot dynamically
adjust similarity results, so for polysemous words, a single embedding model struggles to adapt
to similarity judgments in different contexts.
Therefore, given an embedding model, we need to find a way to dynamically adjust its vector space
so that the similarity calculation results for the same word can differ under different contexts.
Figure 2.9 well demonstrates the practical effect of the word embedding transformation matrix:
by training via machine learning, more suitable transformation matrices are found to achieve
better word embedding performance.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 42

51990.heading: Chapter 2 41
51990.content:
Figure 2.9: Demonstration of the effect of the word embedding transformation matrix
The example above shows why the model needs a way to adjust word representations according
to context. The next question is how the Transformer model learns these transformations. This
is where the query and key weight matrices become important.
Learning the query and key transformation matrices
We can achieve this by training the Q and K weight matrices. The core concept is shown in Figure

Chapter 2 43
In Figure 2.10, some terms are explained as follows:
• Keys: Refers to the Key vectors of the input sequence; each Key vector represents the
semantic information of a word
• Queries: Refers to the Query vectors of the input sequence; each Query vector represents
the semantic information of the word for which the attention weight is currently being
calculated
• Similarity: Refers to the similarity between the Key vector and the Query vector
• Linear Transformation: Refers to applying a linear transformation to the Key and Query
vectors
After the query and key transformations have been introduced, the next step is to see how they
are used inside self-attention. The self-attention mechanism combines queries, keys, and values
to calculate attention weights and produce a context-aware representation of each token.
Explaining the self-attention calculation
During the training process of the self-attention mechanism, the Scaled Dot-Product Attention
mechanism is a very core component. In this mechanism, the model first computes the similarity
between the Q vector and the K vector, then converts the similarity into attention weights via
the Softmax function, and finally multiplies the attention weights by the V vector to obtain the
final output.
Because the attention output depends on the Q, K, and V transformations, these matrices must
be learned during model training. The following subsection explains how the Q and K matrices
are initialized, updated through forward and backward propagation, and optimized to capture
context-specific relationships between tokens.
Training the Q and K weight matrices
Let’s first take a look at the calculation formula for scaled dot-product attention:

Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 44
The computation of scaled dot-product attention is shown in Figure 2.11.
Figure 2.11: Calculation of scaled dot-product attention
As seen in Figure 2.11, the process includes four steps:
1. Word embedding vectors. First, the input words are converted into word embedding
vectors, and then position encoding is added.
2. Q, K, V weight matrices. The word embedding vectors are multiplied by the weight matrices
Q, K, and V, respectively, to obtain the Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V).
3. Calculation of attention weights. The similarity between the Query (Q) and the Key (K) is
calculated, and then the attention weights are obtained by applying the Softmax function.
4. Weighted sum. The attention weights are multiplied by the Value (V), then summed to
get the attention output.

51993.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51993.heading: Chapter 2 45
51993.content:
Chapter 2 45
In the transformer model, the transformation matrices are acquired by training the weight
matrices of Q and K. Specifically, the training process is as follows:
1. Initialization. Randomly initialize the weight matrices for Q and K.
2. Forward propagation
• Map the words in the input sequence to word embedding vectors
• Perform linear transformations on the K and Q vectors to obtain new K and Q
vectors
• Compute the similarity between the K and Q vectors
• Apply Softmax normalization to the similarity scores to obtain the attention
weights
• Perform a weighted sum of the V vectors based on the attention weights to obtain
the final output
3. Backpropagation
• Calculate the loss function
• Update the weight matrices of Q and K based on the loss function
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until training is complete
The goal of this training is to enable the transformer model to learn the similarity relationships
between words in different contexts. For example, in the sentence “Apple phone”, the Transformer
model should be able to learn that there is a higher similarity between “Apple” and “phone.” In
the computation process of the attention mechanism, both the Q vector and the K vector need
to undergo a linear transformation. The weight matrix of the linear transformation is shared,
meaning all words share the same weight matrix. The number of rows in the shared weight matrix
is equal to the size of the vocabulary; for however many words are in the vocabulary, that’s how
many rows are in the shared weight matrix. The number of columns in the shared weight matrix
equals the dimension of the word embedding vectors. The dimension of the word embedding
vectors determines the model’s capacity to express the semantic information of words. In practical
applications, the size of the shared weight matrix may be limited by computational resources.
Some techniques can be used to reduce the size of the shared weight matrix, such as parameter
pruning and knowledge distillation.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 46
Once the training process for the attention weight matrices is clear, the next step is to examine
the actual calculation performed during attention. Scaled dot-product attention explains how
similarity scores are computed, normalized, masked when needed, and then used to produce
the final weighted output.
Understanding scaled dot-product attention
The core principle of the scaled dot-product attention mechanism can be explained in the
following scenarios:
1. Compare the similarity of each word in a sentence with other words. This process is
achieved by computing the dot product between the Q vector of each word and the K
vectors of other words. The result of the dot product represents the similarity between
the two vectors; the higher the value, the greater the similarity. This process can be seen

51994.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51994.heading: Chapter 2 45
51994.content:
as building a similarity matrix between words within a sentence.
The effect of similarity computation is shown in Figure 2.12.
Figure 2.12: Example of similarity calculation based on scaled dot-product attention
(1)

51995.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51995.heading: Chapter 2 47
51995.content:
Chapter 2 47
The left gray box area of Figure 2.12 describes the calculation process of the scaled dot-
product in the formula. The right side of the figure uses the angle between vectors in a two-
dimensional space to represent the similarity between two words. The two-dimensional
vector space undergoes different spatial transformations during the training process
through deep learning.
2. After scaling, masking, and Softmax processing, attention weights are obtained. After
calculating similarity, the model performs scaling processing on the similarity to prevent
values from being too large or too small. Next, the model applies masking to the attention
weights to ensure that the model does not “see” words that have not yet been predicted.
Finally, the model applies Softmax to the scaled similarities to obtain the attention
weights. This process can be viewed as building a matrix of attention weights between
words within the sentence, identifying the key directions of similarity within the sentence
to better capture its semantic information. The effect is shown in Figure 2.13.
Figure 2.13: Example of similarity calculation based on scaled dot-product attention
(2)
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 48
3. Calculate the weighted sum to obtain the final output. After calculating the attention
weights, the model multiplies the attention weights by the value (V) vectors and sums
them to get the final output. This process weights the word embedding vectors, making
their grouping with other phrases more distinct, as shown in Figure 2.14.
Figure 2.14: Example of similarity calculation based on scaled dot-product attention (3)
The result of the vector space transformation in the third step is significantly different from
those in the previous two steps. During the similarity calculation phase, we expect the word
embedding vector space to separate words with different meanings as much as possible, while
in the weighted sum phase, we want similar words to be clustered together to better predict the
probability of the next word. Why is it designed this way? Do you still remember the original intent
of the Transformer model? Its goal is to predict the probability of the next word, which aligns with
the goal of the large language models we use today. The model continuously tries to predict the
next word and adjusts its parameters based on the prediction to better anticipate the next word.

51996.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51996.heading: Chapter 2 49
51996.content:
Chapter 2 49
The output of the self-attention mechanism (i.e., the weighted values) is typically used as
intermediate representations in sequence processing tasks, and these representations are further
processed by subsequent network layers to predict the next word or perform other tasks. Thus,
the self-attention mechanism provides a flexible internal representation, offering each element in
the sequence a contextual representation that synthesizes information from the entire sequence.
The design of the Transformer model nests multiple identical processing layers. Through multi-
level data processing, the self-attention mechanism can capture representations at different
levels, for example, from individual words or characters to more complex semantic concepts
and relationships. Each layer is able to learn more abstract representations of information
from the previous layer’s output. This hierarchical processing helps the model understand the
complex structure of language, including syntactic and semantic information. With multilevel
data processing, the model not only distills information but also integrates and re-encodes
it to generate richer and more complex representations. This process involves capturing and
integrating information from different parts of the sequence to support complex reasoning and
comprehension tasks.
The discussion so far has explained how Transformer self-attention uses learned transformations,
similarity scores, normalization, masking, and weighted sums to build contextual token
representations. The next section extends this idea by showing how the Transformer uses multiple
attention heads in parallel, allowing the model to capture different types of relationships within
the same sequence.
Exploring the design of multi-head attention
In the Transformer model, the multi-head attention mechanism is implemented by combining
multiple attention mechanisms. Each attention mechanism is called a head, and multiple heads
work in parallel, with each head learning different representations. This mechanism enables the
model to focus on different parts of the sequence simultaneously when processing sequences. For
example, some heads may focus on the syntactic structure of the sentence, others may focus on
the semantic information, while others might focus on sentiment information. Through the
multi-head attention mechanism, the model can model sequences from different perspectives,
thereby enhancing its expressive and generalization capabilities.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 50
In the final layer of the model, the outputs of multiple heads are concatenated and then passed
through a linear transformation to obtain the final output. During this process, the model learns
the weights among the different heads in a deep learning manner, as well as how to combine the

51997.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51997.heading: Chapter 2 49
51997.content:
outputs from multiple heads. Building upon what was learned earlier, the following will introduce
the design details of the multi-head attention mechanism.
Figure 2.15: Structure of the multi-head attention mechanism
As shown in Figure 2.15, the multi-head attention mechanism actually consists of the following
three parts:
• Structure of the multi-head attention mechanism � The model is designed with a fixed
number of heads, and each head performs a linear transformation on the input Q, K, and
V. The linear transformations for each head may differ; these are actually implemented
by training weights. Linear transformations allow the model to capture key information
in different embedding spaces. For example, some transformations capture long-range
structural information while others capture short-range dependencies. This design enables
the Transformer model to consider multiple types of dependencies simultaneously when
processing sequential data.

51998.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51998.heading: Chapter 2 51
51998.content:
Chapter 2 51
• Concatenating the attention outputs calculated by each head � The output of each head
is an independent attention vector, which are concatenated to form a long vector. The
reason for concatenating the attention outputs from each head is to merge the different
information captured by each head into a comprehensive representation. Since each head
may focus on different aspects of the input sequence, the concatenation operation allows
the model to utilize this diverse information in subsequent processing. The concatenated
vector contains information from all different heads, which is further integrated by a linear
layer to provide a unified output for downstream tasks. In the original Transformer model,
the number of heads is set to 8, and each head has a dimensionality of 64.
• Integrate information from multi-head attention through linear transformations,
ultimately outputting the attention representation. In the multi-head attention
mechanism, each head can independently learn features regarding the relationships
within the input. The linear layer is responsible for integrating these features, allowing
downstream network layers to utilize information from all heads for decision-making. The
linear layer not only performs weight scaling, but also incorporates non-linear activation
functions (such as ReLU) to enhance the model’s representational power.
Multi-head attention allows the Transformer to examine a sequence from several representational
perspectives at the same time. However, attention is only one part of the full architecture. The next
section brings the components together by showing how embeddings, positional information,
attention layers, feed-forward networks, residual connections, layer normalization, the encoder,
and the decoder form the complete Transformer model.
Assembling the transformer architecture
After examining word embeddings, positional encoding, self-attention, scaled dot-product
attention, and multi-head attention separately, we can now bring these components together
to understand the full Transformer architecture. At a high level, the original Transformer
was designed as an encoder-decoder model for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as machine
translation.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 52
The initial goal of the Transformer model was to build a “language translation” system. The
translation process can be represented as: Input Encoder module Decoder module
Output. The abstract structure of the Transformer is shown in Figure 2.16.
Figure 2.16: Abstract structure of the Transformer
The encoder and decoder are neural network modules that work together to transform an
input sequence into an output sequence. Each module contains multiple encoder and decoder
components. These components are connected in series and can be regarded as a multi-layer

51999.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
51999.heading: Chapter 2 51
51999.content:
homogeneous network. In the earliest papers, this structure consisted of a 6-layer encoder-decoder
architecture. The structures of the Transformer encoder and decoder are shown in Figure 2.17.
Figure 2.17: Transformer encoder and decoder structure
Different Transformer-based models use different parts of this architecture: encoder-only models
such as BERT use the encoder stack, decoder-only models such as GPT use the decoder stack, and
encoder-decoder models use both.

52000.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52000.heading: Chapter 2 53
52000.content:
Chapter 2 53
Each encoder contains multiple submodules, among which the core components are the self-
attention mechanism and the feed-forward neural network. The self-attention mechanism is
used to capture long-range dependencies within the sequence, while the feed-forward neural
network performs non-linear transformations on the information in the sequence. The internal
structure of the Transformer encoder is illustrated in Figure 2.18.
Figure 2.18: Internal structure of the Transformer encoder
The self-attention mechanism enables the model to consider all elements of the entire sequence
when processing each element within the sequence. This allows the model to capture dependencies
between any two elements in the sequence, regardless of their distance from each other. After
the self-attention mechanism captures the dependencies within the sequence, a feedforward
neural network (usually composed of two fully connected layers) independently applies nonlinear
transformations to the representation at each position. The feedforward neural network uses
the same parameters at all positions in the encoder layer, but these parameters are applied
independently to each position. This means that even if the inputs at different positions are the
same, the outputs after passing through the feedforward neural network may still be different.
Additionally, the self-attention layer and the feedforward neural network layer are integrated
through residual connections, which are typically followed by layer normalization to stabilize
training and accelerate convergence.
Summary
In this chapter, you learned why the Transformer model became the foundation of modern large
language models and how it improved on earlier approaches such as RNNs and LSTMs. You saw
that Transformers address major limitations of older sequence models—especially inefficient
sequential processing and difficulty handling long-range dependencies—by using self-attention
and parallel computation.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 54
You were introduced to the core structure of the Transformer, including its encoder-decoder
architecture, and to the major components that make it effective: word embeddings, positional
encoding, self-attention, multi-head attention, feed-forward networks, residual connections,
and layer normalization. You also learned why text must first be converted into numerical form,
how word embeddings capture semantic meaning, and how positional encoding helps preserve
word order.
A major part of the chapter focused on the attention mechanism. You learned how attention helps
the model determine which parts of a sequence are most relevant in context, how Q, K, and V
vectors are used to compute attention, and how scaled dot-product attention and multi-head

52001.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52001.heading: Chapter 2 53
52001.content:
attention enable the model to capture different kinds of relationships within language.
By the end of the chapter, you gained both a conceptual and structural understanding of the
Transformer—not only as a model originally designed for translation, but as the architecture that
powers today’s most important language models. This chapter prepared you to better understand
how modern AI systems process language through contextual understanding, efficient training,
and layered representation learning.
Building on this understanding of the Transformer architecture and its key mechanisms, you
are now ready to explore how this model evolved into modern generative systems. In the next
chapter, you will trace the path from the Transformer to GPT and ChatGPT, beginning with simple
language models such as the bigram model and gradually examining how autoregressive training
and large-scale pretraining enabled today’s conversational AI systems.
3
Tracing the Path from Bigram
Models to GPT and ChatGPT
In the evolution of natural language processing, the birth of the Transformer model marked
a significant turning point for deep learning technology. However, the original Transformer
model was not sufficient to support the generative demands of complex LLMs like ChatGPT. The
emergence of ChatGPT is the result of a gradual evolution based on the Transformer model. By
introducing innovations such as autoregressive pre-training, OpenAI expanded the Transformer
model—originally designed for machine translation—to a broader range of language generation
tasks. In this process, the GPT model, with its unique paradigm of pre-training followed by
fine-tuning and a design specifically aimed at text generation, opened a new chapter for LLMs.
This chapter will guide readers from the basics of bigram models, gradually exploring the core
principles of GPT, and revealing how it evolved step by step into ChatGPT.
We will be covering the following main topics in this chapter:
• Tracing the evolution from transformer to ChatGPT
• Building a basic bigram language model
• Understanding how GPT models generate text
• Improving GPT model training and generation
Tracing the Path from Bigram Models to GPT and ChatGPT 56
Tracing the evolution from transformer to ChatGPT
The original Transformer model was not designed for the kind of multi-turn conversation that
ChatGPT supports today. So how did one evolve into the other? This chapter will start from the
basic principles of the Transformer model, gradually introduce the fundamental concepts of
ChatGPT, and finally explain how to use the ChatGPT model for dialog generation tasks.
The Transformer model was first proposed by Google to solve the problem of machine translation.
This model is based on large-scale parallel corpora (such as English-French sentence pairs)

52002.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52002.heading: Chapter 2 53
52002.content:
and learns by minimizing the cross-entropy loss between the model’s predicted next-token
probabilities and the true next tokens. Based on this, OpenAI proposed the GPT model, extending
the Transformer architecture to a broader range of natural language processing tasks. GPT stands
for Generative Pre-trained Transformer. Like the Transformer, GPT is based on the Transformer
architecture, but its core idea is to use unsupervised pre-training on large-scale corpora to learn
deep language representations, followed by fine-tuning with a small amount of adaptive training
to complete specific downstream tasks. GPT differs structurally from Transformer in that GPT
only uses the decoder part of the Transformer, mainly for generative tasks such as text generation
and dialog generation.
The initial version of the Transformer model was trained on one-to-one parallel corpora,
had limited data, and could only be applied to machine translation tasks. To break through
this limitation, OpenAI proposed a new pre-training method, which trains the model in an
autoregressive manner and combines both masked prediction and next sentence prediction
strategies to enable the model to learn the structure of language directly from large amounts of
unlabeled text. The core idea of autoregressive pre-training is to give a sequence and generate
its elements step by step. This method makes use of large-scale text data and can be applied to
a variety of natural language processing tasks.
Masked prediction means randomly masking some words in the text sequence and requiring
the model to predict the masked words to learn the contextual relationships between words.
Next sentence prediction means that given a text sequence, the model judges whether the
next sentence is related to the given text, helping the model learn logical relationships between
sentences. GPT was the first model to adopt the autoregressive pre-training method and achieved
excellent results. Subsequently, improved models such as BERT and RoBERTa also adopted similar
pre-training methods.

52003.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52003.heading: Chapter 3 57
52003.content:
Chapter 3 57
This chapter focuses on the GPT and ChatGPT models and analyzes them from the following
aspects.
Fine-tuning pre-trained models is a common approach in current LLM applications. The GPT
model adopts a pre-training plus fine-tuning paradigm, which was subsequently widely applied
to various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Pre-trained models learn general language
characteristics from large-scale corpora and are then fine-tuned on specific tasks, significantly
improving the model’s performance and efficiency.
LLMs have a wide range of applications. GPT and its subsequent versions have demonstrated
outstanding performance on various natural language processing tasks, including text generation,
translation, summarization, question answering, and more. This shows that a single pre-trained
model, through fine-tuning, can be adapted to multiple tasks, significantly enhancing the model’s
versatility and flexibility.
The consensus is that the larger the number of parameters, the more powerful the capability. The
latest GPT model, with its enormous scale, has showcased the potential of LLMs in understanding
and generating natural language, driving the development of large-scale language model research
and sparking widespread discussions about the possible impacts of LLMs.
Next, a bigram model will be introduced as the starting point for language model training. Then,
the basic principles of the GPT model will be described, including the structure of GPT, pre-
training methods, and so on.
Building a basic bigram language model
The Bigram Model is one of the simplest language models. Based on the Markov assumption, it
assumes that the occurrence of a word is only related to the previous word. The core of the Bigram
Model is that, given a text sequence, the model needs to predict the next word.
When training the model, how can text be converted into numbers that can be computed? A
common method is to construct a dictionary that maps characters or words to numerical indexes.
In this way, the text sequence can be transformed into a sequence of numbers and input into the
model for training. During model prediction, numeric indexes can be converted back to characters
or words to obtain the model’s output.
Tracing the Path from Bigram Models to GPT and ChatGPT 58
This method is widely used in natural language processing and is fundamental to building text
datasets. This example uses character-level tokenization for simplicity. In this approach, each
character is treated as a token and mapped to a numerical index. This works reasonably well for
demonstrating the basic mechanics of language-model training, especially with Chinese text,
where individual characters can carry meaningful information. However, production GPT-style
models usually do not rely on simple character-level tokenization. Instead, they typically use

52004.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52004.heading: Chapter 3 57
52004.content:
subword tokenization methods such as Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), WordPiece, or SentencePiece,
which split text into reusable word pieces and handle large vocabularies more efficiently. For
real applications, libraries such as tiktoken or sentencepiece can be used to implement more
practical tokenization workflows.
The following sample demonstrates how to convert text into numerical indexes. Collect the file
“Three Hundred Tang Poems”, which contains multiple poems from the Tang Dynasty. The goal
is to train a model so that it can automatically generate Tang poetry.
The training data is as follows: each Tang poem is treated as a sentence, and these sentences are
concatenated to form a long text. The input to the model is this long text, and the objective is to
predict the next word. Issues to be solved in the process include how to convert text to numbers,
how to design the model, and how to train the model.
The first step in this workflow is data representation. Before the model can learn from text, the
text must be converted into numerical form so that it can be processed by the neural network.
The following subsection shows how the corpus is read, how the character vocabulary is created,
and how characters are mapped to numerical indices.
This chapter uses Three Hundred Tang Poems as a small character-level text corpus to
demonstrate the mechanics of language-model training. To make the example easier
for readers to follow, the Tang poetry referenced in the explanation and generated
examples has been translated into English. The same workflow can be applied to
other text corpora as well; for example, readers may use an English public-domain
corpus such as Shakespeare’s works or WikiText-2 by changing the dataset path,
tokenization choices, and generated text examples.

Chapter 3 59
How text is converted to numbers
First, let’s explore the data of 300 Tang Poems. The relevant code is as follows:

Next, establish a mapping table from characters to numbers to convert text into numbers. At the
same time, in order to convert the predicted numbers back to characters, a mapping table from
numbers to characters is also required. The mapping table is shown below:
# Build the mapping from characters to numbers and from numbers to
characters

indices_char = dict((i, c) for i, c in enumerate(chars))
# Basic function for converting text into numbers
def text_to_indices(text):
return [char_indices[c] for c in text]
def indices_to_text(indices):
return ''.join(indices_char[i] for i in indices)
After the text has been converted into numerical indexes, the next step is to define a model that
can learn from those indexes. In a bigram language model, the design is intentionally simple:
the model receives the current token, converts it into an embedding, and predicts the next token.
This simple structure makes it easier to understand the basic prediction loop before moving on
to GPT-style models.
How to design the model
How can an LLM automatically generate a piece of poetry? Similar to ChatGPT, generating a
paragraph of text according to instructions is relatively complex, so the goal can be simplified to:
“Give a random word as input, and let the LLM automatically generate a new poem.” Recalling
the text generation effect of the LLM used, does it output word by word? The process of gradually
generating the same sentence is actually a continuous prediction process.

The result after each prediction is used as input and added to the next prediction, forming a loop.
Thus, the text generation process of a LLM is essentially a continuous prediction process. This
prediction process can be abstracted as a model whose input is a word and whose output is the
next word. The structure of this model is a neural network: the input of the neural network is a
word, and its output is the next word.
In this example, the model is implemented at the character level for simplicity: each
character is treated as a token, and the model predicts the next character rather than
the next full word. This is convenient for demonstrating the mechanics of token
mapping, embedding, training, and generation. In production LLMs, however, text is
usually processed with subword tokenizers such as BPE, WordPiece, or SentencePiece,
which split text into reusable word pieces rather than individual characters.

Chapter 3 61
Starting from a simple bigram model, the input is one token, and the output is the next token.
The statistical formula involved in the traditional bigram model is as follows:
𝑃𝑃( 𝑤𝑤𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡 ∣ ∣ 𝑤𝑤𝑡𝑡 ) = {𝑃𝑃(𝑤𝑤𝑡𝑡, 𝑤𝑤𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡)/𝑃𝑃(𝑤𝑤𝑡𝑡)} 
Here, w t is the input word, and w t+1 is the output word. This formula means that given a word w t,
we need to predict the probability that the next word w t+1 appears. This probability consists of
two parts: the numerator is the probability that w t and w t+1 occur together, and the denominator
is the probability that w t appears.
From the neural network implementation perspective, a bigram model usually uses an embedding
layer to convert vocabulary into dense vector representations, followed by one or more linear
layers (possibly including activation functions) to predict the probability distribution of the
next word. The model may also include a Softmax layer to convert outputs into a probability
distribution. This process is mathematically represented as follows:
𝑧𝑧𝑧𝑧𝑧𝑧 𝑧 𝑧𝑁𝑁𝑁𝑁(𝑣𝑣 𝑧 𝑣 𝑧 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 𝑧𝑧𝑧 | 𝑃𝑃𝑧𝑧 𝑧 𝑧 𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤 (𝑧𝑧𝑧𝑧𝑧𝑣 
Among them, v t is the embedding vector of the input word w t, NN is the neural network, z t+1 is
the output of the neural network, 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃ₜ₊₁| 𝑃𝑃ₜ  is the probability distribution for the next word w t+1.
This formula indicates that given a word w t, it predicts the probability distribution of the next
word w t+1. This probability distribution is computed by the neural network NN and transformed
into a probability distribution via the Softmax function.
A bigram model predicts the next token using only the immediately previous token. Although
this is much simpler than GPT, it is a useful starting point because it has the same basic input-
output pattern: the model receives token IDs, converts them into embeddings, and predicts the
next token. Training this simple model helps build intuition for tokenization, embedding layers,
cross-entropy loss, and the repeated prediction loop that GPT later extends with attention and
deeper Transformer blocks.
Below is a code implementation of a simple bigram model. The code consists of four parts: model
preparation, parameter initialization, training process, and generation process.

from torch.nn import functional as F
# Set hyperparameters

def get_batch(data, batch_size):
