5
Building Enterprise AI
Applications with RAG and
Multi-Agent Systems
Modern LLMs (GPT-5, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, and others) have profoundly
transformed the field of natural language processing, bringing about numerous breakthroughs.
However, these models often face a range of challenges when addressing specific enterprise needs,
especially in terms of data security, accuracy, and domain expertise.
Against this backdrop, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) technology has emerged. By
combining traditional information retrieval with advanced text generation, this technology
effectively enhances model performance and applicability in specific business scenarios. This
chapter aims to systematically introduce the working principles of RAG technology and its
application cases in enterprises, helping readers gain an in-depth understanding of how to deploy
this technology in daily business operations.
In this chapter, we will be covering the following topics:
• Understanding the core workflow of RAG
• Addressing enterprise constraints with RAG
• Applying RAG to enterprise question-answering scenarios
• Generating SQL with RAG2SQL
• Coordinating complex tasks with multi-agent systems
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 138
Understanding the core workflow of RAG
RAG is one of the most important patterns for building enterprise-ready LLM applications because
it allows a model to generate answers using external, organization-specific knowledge rather
than relying only on what it learned during training. To understand how RAG works, it is useful
to begin with its two core components—the retriever and the generator—and then examine how
data moves through the indexing, retrieval, and generation stages of the workflow.
Core components of RAG
RAG is a natural language processing technology that combines information retrieval and text
generation. By integrating information from large-scale datasets, RAG enhances the output of
generative models, enabling them to provide more comprehensive, accurate, and detailed answers.
This technology has broad application potential in areas such as question answering systems,
chatbots, and content generation.
Its core components include the Retriever and the Generator:
• The Retriever is responsible for quickly retrieving the most relevant information from vast
document collections or datasets based on the user’s query. It uses efficient indexing and
query techniques, such as inverted indexes or the latest vector search methods, to ensure
that the most relevant results are returned in the shortest possible time.

52075.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52075.heading: Chapter 4 133
52075.content:
• The Generator is responsible for generating coherent, relevant, and information-rich text
based on the retrieved information. Advanced language models such as GPT or BERT are
commonly used, combined with the content from retrieved documents, to generate text
directly related to the user’s query.
Together, the retriever and generator form the foundation of a RAG system. The retriever identifies
the information most relevant to the user’s query, while the generator uses that information to
produce a grounded response. The next step is to look at how these components work together
across the full RAG workflow.

52076.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52076.heading: Chapter 5 139
52076.content:
Chapter 5 139
RAG workflow
The RAG workflow is shown in Figure 5.1 and is divided into the data indexing stage, retrieval
stage, and generation stage.
Figure 5.1: RAG workflow
1. Data indexing stage
The data indexing stage mainly uses embedding models to convert different types of data into
vectors and store them in a vector database. Common vector database choices include Milvus
and Weaviate (self-hosted, open source), Pinecone (managed cloud), and pgvector (PostgreSQL
extension for teams already using Postgres). LlamaIndex and LangChain support all of these
via consistent interfaces. For text data, use a dedicated embedding model trained for retrieval
— sentence-transformers (open source), OpenAI text-embedding-3 (commercial), or BGE-M3
(open source, multilingual). Plain BERT is a feature extractor and underperforms purpose-built
embedding models on retrieval tasks.
2. Retrieval stage
In the retrieval stage, the user’s input query is converted into a vector, which is then matched for
similarity with the data in the vector database to find the most relevant data.
1. Document segmentation: First, long textual documents in large-scale datasets are
segmented into smaller, more manageable, and easily searchable chunks
2. Semantic similarity check: Natural language processing tools are used to analyze
the semantic similarity between the user’s query and each document chunk, quickly
pinpointing the most relevant information
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 140
Once the most relevant document chunks have been retrieved, the system can pass them to the
generator to produce a response grounded in the retrieved context.
3. Generation stage
In the generation stage, the retrieved data is passed to the generator, which produces the final
output based on the retrieved data and the user’s query.
1. Text Matching and Relevance: Based on retrieval results, the generator evaluates the
relevance of the information and constructs answers according to the user’s specific needs
2. Diversity and Uniqueness: When generating answers, focus is placed on the diversity
and uniqueness of content to avoid generating generic or repetitive text, ensuring output
quality and personalization
In addition, even for text data, there are various file formats, such as Text, Word, PDF, etc., which
require different processing methods. Currently, LlamaIndex provides a variety of tools to
conveniently handle these different file formats.
After understanding the basic RAG workflow, the next question is why enterprises need this
approach in the first place. RAG is especially useful in business environments where models must
work with private data, produce evidence-based answers, and apply domain-specific knowledge
that may not be available in the model’s original training data.

52077.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52077.heading: Chapter 5 139
52077.content:
Addressing enterprise constraints with RAG
Enterprise application scenarios usually include three types of constraints: data security
requirements, data accuracy requirements, and domain knowledge requirements:
• Data security requirements: Enterprises usually possess large amounts of data with strict
data security requirements that must not be disclosed to external parties
• Data accuracy requirements: The output of LLMs must be evidence-based
• Domain knowledge requirements: The meaning represented by enterprise data is often
unique to vertical domains, making it difficult for general LLMs to provide answers based
on domain knowledge

52078.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52078.heading: Chapter 5 141
52078.content:
Chapter 5 141
The advantages of RAG technology are shown in Figure 5.2.
Figure 5.2: Advantages of RAG technology
As shown in Figure 5.2, RAG is useful because it connects three elements that are often difficult to
align in enterprise AI applications: the user’s intent, the knowledge already contained in the LLM,
and external enterprise data. Without retrieval, an LLM may generate plausible but unsupported
answers, increasing the risk of hallucination. Without an intent-aware search layer, enterprise data
may remain difficult to retrieve accurately, even when the relevant information exists. Without
RAG, organizations may also rely too heavily on fine-tuning, which can introduce additional
cost, hardware requirements, and maintenance overhead. By retrieving relevant external data at
query time and providing it to the model as context, RAG helps generate answers that are more
grounded, accurate, and aligned with enterprise-specific knowledge.
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 142
Under the three types of constraints mentioned above, RAG technology can effectively address
enterprise pain points and meet their needs.
After explaining why RAG is well suited to enterprise constraints, the next step is to see how it
works in practical business scenarios. Question-answering systems are a natural starting point
because they require the model to understand user intent, retrieve relevant enterprise knowledge,
and generate responses that are accurate, contextual, and useful to the user.
Applying RAG to enterprise question-answering
scenarios
RAG is especially useful in enterprise question-answering scenarios because it allows an LLM
to retrieve relevant business knowledge before generating a response. This section looks at two
examples: a customer service Q&A system that uses historical voice and answer data, and a
wealth management assistant that helps client managers retrieve and apply financial, product,
and customer information.
Building a customer service Q&A system
A certain bank has accumulated a large amount of customer service Q&A voice data over the past
several years, containing customers’ questions and customer service responses. The bank hopes
to leverage this data to build an intelligent customer service Q&A system to help customers solve
problems more quickly and accurately.
(1) Speech recognition
Converting customer voice input into text data is the first step of the process, as the original voice
data needs to be transformed into text for subsequent processing and understanding. By using
existing high-accuracy speech recognition technologies, such as the API service interface from the
OpenAI Whisper API, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, or Microsoft Azure Speech, or offline models
such as Whisper or Distil-Whisper for self-hosted deployments, customers’ spoken questions

52079.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52079.heading: Chapter 5 141
52079.content:
can be transcribed into text.
(2) Text preprocessing
Cleaning and standardizing the text data after speech recognition includes removing stop
words, correcting spelling errors, and standardizing grammar. First, leverage the contextual
understanding capabilities of LLMs to fix obvious errors; second, further improve the quality and
accuracy of the text through manual proofreading.

52080.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52080.heading: Chapter 5 143
52080.content:
Chapter 5 143
(3) Applying RAG technology
Apply RAG technology, which combines retrieval and generation, to first retrieve the most relevant
content from a large-scale knowledge base, and then generate answers based on this content. This
process is realized through two stages. The first stage is to construct a question bank and a standard
answer bank, quickly finding standard answers most related to the question through retrieval
techniques. In this process, LLMs are used to generate multiple similar questions, improving
retrieval coverage. The second stage is to use the comprehension ability of LLMs to retrieve the
customer’s own information (such as purchased product information, latest interaction records,
etc.) based on the question.
(4) Generating answers
The purpose of answer generation is to produce accurate and human-friendly responses, and
to achieve personalized feedback based on the retrieval results, allowing the model to continue
training to adapt to specific business and language usage, thereby improving the relevance and
accuracy of the responses.
(5) Post-processing and feedback loop
Through post-processing and a feedback loop, response quality, and system performance can
be optimized. This involves grammar correction and style adjustment for generated answers to
ensure professionalism and accuracy. At the same time, feedback on customer satisfaction with
the answers is sent back into the system for continual learning and improvement of the model.
The same RAG pattern can also be applied beyond customer service. In knowledge-intensive
domains such as wealth management, RAG can help professionals retrieve client information,
product details, market knowledge, and past interaction records to support more personalized
responses.
Supporting wealth management with RAG
In the field of wealth management, RAG has a wide range of applications, from client managers’
customer management to clients’ wealth management, and all can utilize RAG technology.
The following takes the pain points of a client manager as an example to describe the specific
application of RAG in this field. The background is: Alice Summers is a wealth client manager at
a financial institution, responsible for managing the contact information of over 1,000 clients.
Her customer management tasks mainly include the following:
• Regularly contacting clients to understand their latest needs and investment intentions
• Providing personalized investment advice based on clients’ needs and risk preferences

• Timely answering clients’ questions and resolving their issues
• Regularly sending clients the latest financial market news and investment advice
• Tracking clients’ investment situations to adjust portfolios in a timely manner

• Focusing on vertical application scenarios performs better than generalized scenarios.
Through wealth product evaluation, when data and metrics are clearly defined, the

• Clarify the requirements for models and hardware resources. A model with 7.2 billion

Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 148
After looking at how RAG can support enterprise question-answering scenarios, the chapter now
turns to a more structured data problem: generating SQL from natural language questions. In
many organizations, valuable business information is stored in databases, but users often need
knowledge of table structures, field meanings, and query logic to access it. RAG2SQL applies the
retrieval-and-generation pattern to this problem by combining database metadata, historical SQL
examples, and natural language understanding to help generate SQL that matches enterprise-
specific data logic.
Generating SQL with RAG2SQL
Text-to-SQL refers to the process of converting a user’s natural language question into a SQL
query that can be executed against a structured database. For example, a user might ask, “Which
products had the highest sales last quarter?” and the system must translate that request into a
valid SQL statement that selects the right tables, fields, filters, and aggregation logic. This task
is more difficult than ordinary text retrieval because the model must understand both the user’s
intent and the database schema, then produce SQL that is syntactically correct and consistent
with the organization’s business rules.
Generating SQL from natural language is one of the more structured applications of RAG because
the model must understand both the user’s question and the organization’s database logic. Unlike
general text generation, RAG2SQL depends on schema information, metadata, business definitions,

52084.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52084.heading: Chapter 5 147
52084.content:
historical SQL examples, and result validation. This section explains why enterprise text-to-SQL
is difficult, then uses Vanna AI as an example framework to show how RAG can support SQL
generation, workflow design, domain-specific retrieval, and iterative improvement.
Understanding the enterprise Text-to-SQL problem
With the rise of LLM technology, programmers have been among the first to experience the
revolutionary changes in code development, ranging from autocompletion to the automatic
generation of module functionalities. However, in the database domain, despite its vast potential,
there have not yet been breakthrough advances. The main challenges lie in the diversity and
complexity of enterprise databases: each company’s database structure, table design, and
statistical processing logic are unique, and this information is seldom shared on open-source
platforms such as GitHub.
To address these challenges, organizations can combine locally deployed LLMs, database metadata,
business definitions, and historical SQL examples in a RAG workflow. This allows the system to
retrieve relevant schema information and prior query patterns before generating SQL that aligns
with enterprise-specific business logic. The widespread application of this technology will bring
great convenience to data analysts and big data platform operations and management personnel.

52085.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52085.heading: Chapter 5 149
52085.content:
Chapter 5 149
Using Vanna AI as a RAG2SQL example
Currently, the open-source software provider Vanna � ai has released its foundational RAG2SQL
framework on GitHub. This framework achieves high-precision SQL generation on complex
datasets through several key features:
• RAG framework: By integrating retrieval-augmented generation technology, it enhances
the accuracy of generated SQL statements
• LLMs: Utilize advanced LLMs to understand complex query requirements
• High-quality training data: Trained on abundant data to improve the quality of generated
SQL statements
• Continuous optimization capabilities: The framework supports continual learning and
optimization to adapt to ever-changing data environments
• Broad database support: Compatible with various types of databases and frontend
technologies
• Open-source customization: Allows users to customize and optimize the framework
based on specific requirements
The Vanna AI framework has wide-ranging application scenarios, covering business intelligence,
medical research, education, and other fields, suitable for any situation that requires efficient
data query and analysis. With improvements in natural language processing capabilities, users
can submit query requests in natural language, which the system automatically translates into
SQL statements and executes in the database to retrieve the required data.
Following the RAG2SQL workflow
These capabilities come together in a workflow that retrieves relevant schema, metadata, and
SQL examples before generating and validating a query.
Several frameworks can be used to explore this pattern. The following discussion
uses Vanna AI as one representative open-source example of how RAG can be applied
to natural language-to-SQL generation.
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 150
The workflow of RAG2SQL based on the Vanna AI framework is shown in Figure 5.7.
Figure 5.7: Workflow of RAG2SQL based on the Vanna AI framework
This system is used to convert natural language queries into SQL queries, which are executed
to obtain data, and then the results are validated and processed. The workflow consists of the
following main steps:
1. Raise the Question: The user raises a question, which is the starting point of the process
2. Search: The system searches for relevant information by querying databases, documents,
or other stored answers. This step may involve accessing data indexes and can use vector
searches or other advanced search technologies.
3. Prompt Generation: Based on the information found during the search, the system
generates one or more SQL query prompts. This could involve understanding and parsing
natural language queries, then converting them into structured queries.
4. Execute SQL Query: The system constructs SQL queries based on the generated prompts

52086.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52086.heading: Chapter 5 149
52086.content:
and executes them on the database. The database here can be any data storage system
that supports SQL.

52087.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52087.heading: Chapter 5 151
52087.content:
Chapter 5 151
5. Result Verification: The system presents the query results to the user and checks whether
the user’s needs are met. This may include data frames, charts, or AI-generated follow-
up questions.
6. Result Feedback: If the results are correct, the process ends and the user obtains the
required information; if not, the user can perform a manual query or rewrite the question,
and the system may learn and adjust according to the feedback
After the overall workflow is clear, it is useful to look more closely at the RAG-specific features
that support SQL generation and domain knowledge retrieval.
Examining RAG-specific features
Under this framework, Vanna AI has implemented two features:
• A RAG model is trained based on provided SQL historical code. The entire process requires
manual problem construction, restoring the code’s function into natural language
descriptions, as shown in Figure 5.8.
Figure 5.8: SQL code generation process
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 152
• A RAG-based domain knowledge information retrieval tool is constructed, for example,
using various business metadata and statistical metric descriptions from big data systems.
To improve retrieval accuracy, an additional classification model is trained to identify
the information category associated with each query and to further retrieve and provide
accurate information to the LLM based on the classification results. The RAG2SQL retrieval
filtering process is shown in Figure 5.9.
Figure 5.9: RAG2SQL retrieval filtering process
Although this framework shows how RAG can support SQL generation, practical deployment
still depends on framework maturity, model access, metadata quality, annotation effort, and the
surrounding AI infrastructure.
Recognizing current system limitations
The current system also has some shortcomings or areas to be optimized, mainly in the following
aspects:
• Currently, the framework is in its initial stage, and the functional modules are not yet
complete or robust.
• It relies on API-based calls to commercial LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google),
which may not be available or affordable in all deployment environments. Self-hosted
alternatives (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, or other open-weight models) require additional
integration work that the framework does not yet provide out of the box.

52088.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52088.heading: Chapter 5 153
52088.content:
Chapter 5 153
• Cost and latency should also be considered when choosing a deployment model. As a
rough order-of-magnitude estimate, a lightweight commercial-API RAG query that uses
an embedding model plus a small or mid-sized LLM may cost around $0.001–$0.005 per
query and return in about 1–3 seconds, depending on prompt length, retrieved context
size, model choice, and network conditions. A self-hosted equivalent using an open-
source embedding model and an open-weight LLM can reduce marginal per-query cost
after infrastructure is in place, but it requires GPU capacity, deployment engineering,
monitoring, scaling, and ongoing maintenance.
• The training process involves quite a few data governance factors, such as the completeness
of metadata.
• During training, many samples require manual annotation, such as reverse-translating
code into natural language descriptions, etc.
• Relying on relatively complete AI foundational platforms, such as vector data, embedding
model selection, customized classification model design and training, etc.
If the above issues can be resolved, the implementation of RAG2SQL technology will bring
tremendous long-term value.
Several of the RAG2SQL challenges discussed above involve coordinating multiple steps, including
retrieval, prompt generation, SQL execution, result verification, feedback, metadata management,
and integration with supporting tools. These are exactly the kinds of multi-step workflows that
multi-agent frameworks are designed to help organize. The next section introduces multi-agent
systems and shows how a framework such as CrewAI can structure a pipeline in which different
agents take on different roles, use tools, pass outputs to one another, and collaborate toward a
final result.
Coordinating complex tasks with multi-agent systems
The RAG2SQL framework workflow covers multiple tasks, from data sample preparation and
classification model training to generated result evaluation. Currently, the latest LLMs are
attempting to automate various processes through multi-agent systems. There are already
more than a dozen multi-agent systems, such as Microsoft’s AutoGen, LangChain agents (built
using the LangChain framework), CrewAI, etc. These systems share the common feature of
decomposing the output of LLMs into multiple tasks, each accomplished by different agents.
This method can improve the efficiency and accuracy of the system, while better adapting to
different business scenarios.
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 154
Using CrewAI as an example multi-agent framework
In some scenarios, this concept has already seen initial applications. Figure 5.10 shows an
application case of the CrewAI framework.
Figure 5.10: Application case of the CrewAI framework
CrewAI is a multi-agent system framework that allows developers to create teams composed

52089.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52089.heading: Chapter 5 153
52089.content:
of multiple agents that can collaborate to accomplish complex tasks. The design of the CrewAI
framework is inspired by human team collaboration, where each agent can take on different roles
and focus on specific tasks or domains. Below are some key features of the CrewAI framework:
• Role-playing agents: In CrewAI, each agent is assigned a role, such as database expert,
technical writer, or quality assurance specialist, and performs tasks according to its role
and objectives
Several frameworks can be used to build multi-agent workflows, including AutoGen,
LangChain agents, CrewAI, and similar orchestration tools. The following example
uses CrewAI as a representative framework because it clearly shows how agents,
tasks, tools, and processes can be combined into a collaborative workflow.

52090.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52090.heading: Chapter 5 155
52090.content:
Chapter 5 155
• Task definition: Developers can define specific tasks for each agent, such as task
descriptions, expected output, available tools, and allocation
• Tool usage: Agents can utilize predefined tools or custom tools to accomplish tasks, such as
searching the internet, parsing websites, or performing document retrieval and generation
• Process control: CrewAI provides various process control options, including sequential
execution, hierarchical management, and consensus mechanisms, to coordinate task
execution among the agents
• Memory mechanism: CrewAI supports different types of memory, including short-term
memory, long-term memory, and entity memory, to facilitate effective collaboration and
knowledge sharing among agents
• Easy to Use: CrewAI is designed to simplify the usage and setup process, allowing
developers to quickly build prototypes and iterate on solutions
• Flexibility and Scalability: CrewAI supports flexible task allocation and agent
collaboration, adapting to various business problems and requirements
• Built-in Best Practices: CrewAI encourages the use of best practices such as role-playing
and clear task definitions to improve system efficiency and reliability
• Environment Integration: CrewAI can be integrated with external environments such
as the OpenAI API, and can also be used with local models
• Error Handling and Robustness: CrewAI provides error handling mechanisms to help
agents recover when encountering problems
After introducing CrewAI’s main features, the next step is to see how these concepts appear in
a simple workflow. The following example uses three agents—a researcher, a writer, and an
editor—to show how multi-agent systems can divide work, pass outputs between roles, and
produce a final result through sequential collaboration.
Applying CrewAI to a sequential agent workflow
Below is an example of applying the CrewAI framework to collect and generate technical log blogs:
1. Environment Preparation: Install Ollama, CrewAI, crewai_tools, and LangChain locally
(the author has a workstation with a consumer-grade GPU, and the software includes
Ollama and Llama 3 quantized version)
2. WebAPI Preparation: Visit https://serper.dev to obtain free API usage and API key
information. This service is used for Web search functionality via API calls.

Interpreting the CrewAI workflow
An application summary of CrewAI is as follows:
1. The CrewAI agent framework includes the following four core components:
• Task: The specific task to be executed by the agent. In this example, the task is
“write a technical blog”.
• Agent: The AI agent that performs the task. Each agent specializes in different
tasks, such as the researcher, writer, and editor expert roles in this example.
• Tool: Tools used by agents when executing tasks, such as search engines,
summarizers, translators, etc. In this example, the tool is SerperDevTool, which
is used for web information search.
• Process: The way agents collaborate to work, for example, sequential processes
or hierarchical processes. In this case, the agents execute the task in a sequential
process. The process can be flexibly adjusted according to different situations.
2. To accomplish the entire task, agents use LLMs to think and act in order to complete the
task. For example, the following output is the result of the agent’s reasoning:
Entering new CrewAgentExecutor chain...
Thought: Where do I start?

3. The tools used by the agent can be external APIs or internally customized service
components, allowing the agent to interact with them in a standardized way. For example,
in this case, SerperDevTool is used for web information search. Custom tools can also be
used, such as document parsers, data cleaners, etc.
4. Agents can delegate tasks to other agents, and ask each other questions based on context,
in order to achieve collaborative work and jointly complete complex tasks. For example,
in this case, research information found by the researcher can be directly passed to the
writer, who then writes a blog based on this information.
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 162
Together, these points show that the value of a multi-agent framework does not come from
the LLM alone. It comes from the way tasks, agents, tools, and processes are organized into a
coordinated workflow. Once this pattern is understood, it becomes easier to see how the same
approach can be extended beyond this simple CrewAI example to broader enterprise scenarios.
Recognizing the broader value of multi-agent systems
The current agent framework is already capable of enabling multi-agent collaboration to complete

complex tasks. This framework can be applied to many fields, such as natural language processing,
data analysis, knowledge graph construction, etc. In the future, as LLMs develop and agent
frameworks continue to improve, it is foreseeable that more collaborative work among agents
will be realized, thus enabling the completion of even more complex tasks.
Summary
In this chapter, you explored the fundamentals of RAG and its role in building enterprise-ready
AI applications. You learned how RAG enhances LLMs by integrating external knowledge sources,
enabling more accurate, context-aware, and up-to-date responses. The chapter walked you
through the core architecture of RAG systems, including data ingestion, embedding, retrieval,
and generation, along with key optimization techniques to improve retrieval quality and system
performance. You also examined practical implementation approaches, common tools and
frameworks, and real-world use cases that demonstrate how RAG can be applied in enterprise
environments such as customer support, knowledge management, and data-driven decision-
making.
Building on these concepts, the next chapter shifts focus to the broader software delivery ecosystem,
where you will learn how DevOps, platform engineering, and SRE work together as foundational
pillars to enable scalable, reliable, and efficient deployment of AI-powered systems in real-world
enterprise settings.
6
Building a Modern Software
Delivery Foundation
From development to implementation, software must go through several stages, including
requirements design, development, testing, and deployment. During the collaboration process,
data silos and system silos exist between each stage, inevitably leading to conflicts. Furthermore,
collaboration issues between different capability subdomains are also common in many enterprises.
DevOps, SRE (Site Reliability Engineering), and Platform Engineering serve as the three
foundational cornerstones of software delivery. Like links in a chain, they orchestrate engineers’
work across different platforms, enabling multi-platform collaboration and allowing engineers to
complete software delivery more efficiently and enjoyably. In addition, they provide enterprises
with a range of objective data, allowing for real-time analysis of weak links in the delivery process,
accelerating software time-to-market, and enabling quick response to market demands.
In this chapter, the main headings will be:
• Improving software delivery with DevOps
• Building internal platforms for software delivery
• Strengthening system reliability with SRE
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 164
Improving software delivery with DevOps
DevOps is one of the main foundations of modern software delivery because it connects the people,
processes, tools, and feedback loops involved in turning software ideas into reliable business value.

52096.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52096.heading: Chapter 5 161
52096.content:
Rather than treating development, testing, operations, and business teams as separate groups
working in sequence, DevOps encourages them to collaborate across the full delivery lifecycle. In
this section, we examine how DevOps supports enterprise goals, connects IT capability domains,
improves delivery visibility, shifts quality and risk management earlier in the lifecycle, strengthens
digital operations, and extends into newer practices such as MLOps and LLMOps.
The three pillars discussed in this chapter are practices and operating models rather
than single tools. In real organizations, they are usually implemented through a
combination of automation, infrastructure, observability, incident management,
and internal-platform tools. The following examples provide a practical starting
point for readers who want to connect these concepts to commonly used tooling:
Figure 6.1: Tools commonly used across DevOps, Platform Engineering,
and SRE
The key point is that DevOps, platform engineering, and SRE are implemented
through toolchains that support collaboration, self-service, automation, observ -
ability, and reliability.

52097.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52097.heading: Chapter 6 165
52097.content:
Chapter 6 165
The concept of DevOps
DevOps (a combination of Development and Operations) is a collective term for the processes,
methods, and systems used to facilitate communication, collaboration, and integration between
software development, IT operations, and quality assurance departments, as shown in Figure 6.2.
Professionals in the software industry have gradually realized that, in order to deliver software
products or services on time, developers and operations staff must work closely together, focus
on communication, and speed up, reliably build, test, and release software through automated
processes.
Figure 6.2: Scope of DevOps
In recent years, DevOps has been implemented across various industries, sectors, and enterprises
of different sizes, achieving good practical results. For enterprises aiming at lean operation and IT
lean management, the original concepts of DevOps can no longer meet their needs, giving rise to
disruptive development and transformation. Improving organizational-level efficiency and quality
has become a new direction for capabilities output in the development of DevOps. Therefore,
besides its original role in facilitating inter-departmental communication, DevOps now elevates
full lifecycle management of applications to a new level. At the same time, corresponding cultural
collaboration and process-driven approaches have advanced alongside data-driven capabilities,
achieving a highly collaborative goal in technical operations and value delivery.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 166
For enterprise users, it is essential to clearly explain what DevOps is, what its core objectives are,
and what capabilities should be possessed, as this directly relates to enterprise-level practice
and implementation. The author has discussed with members and individuals from multiple
relevant organizations in the industry, and though their feedback varied, the core value remains
consistent—how to achieve ultimate value delivery and output through DevOps.
To understand this value more clearly, DevOps needs to be viewed not only as a technical practice
but also as an enterprise capability. Its impact depends on how well it supports business goals
and how effectively IT organizations use it to coordinate delivery, operations, and continuous
improvement.
The relationship among DevOps, enterprises, and IT
organizations
DevOps sits between enterprise strategy and IT execution. At the enterprise level, it helps
organizations improve delivery speed, quality, and responsiveness to market needs. At the IT
organization level, it provides a way to coordinate teams, standardize processes, automate delivery
activities, and create feedback loops across the software lifecycle. The following discussion looks
at both relationships in turn.
The relationship between DevOps and enterprises

52098.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52098.heading: Chapter 6 165
52098.content:
The development of enterprises requires clear goals, which are usually measured by economic
benefits. Economic benefits include productivity, turnover, profit margin, and return on investment.
The development goals of an enterprise can be described from the following four aspects:
• The enterprise’s contribution goals to society. For different types and business models of
enterprises, the enterprise’s contribution goals to society are reflected in the effectiveness
and benefits of their products.
• The enterprise’s market goals. The market goals determine whether an enterprise can
survive. Improving the innovation level of products, the ability to bring products to market
quickly, and a product’s market share are important means to achieve the enterprise’s
market goals.
• The enterprise’s development goals. The development goals are key for enterprises to
improve productivity. They are achieved by expanding enterprise scale, increasing fixed
assets and working capital, enhancing production capacity, increasing product variety,
output, and sales, improving per capita productivity, and raising automation levels.

52099.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52099.heading: Chapter 6 167
52099.content:
Chapter 6 167
• The enterprise’s profit goals. In the course of business operations, an enterprise aims to
maximize its profit goals through cost reduction and efficiency enhancement. “Cost
reduction and efficiency enhancement” can be achieved by product adjustments and
internal management changes, based on internal and external data analysis and support.
The positioning of DevOps in enterprise development is more about creating added value
than achieving miracles in desperate situations. When implementing enterprise-level DevOps,
managers should note that regardless of whether the enterprise is undergoing business model
transformation, digital transformation, or brand management transformation, it must use
advanced information technology to enhance management levels and improve competitiveness—
this is precisely the value and capability that DevOps provides.
In terms of core value output, DevOps acts as a “catalyst,” which does not conflict with the
enterprise’s development goals. Therefore, regardless of whether DevOps implementation is
successful, it will not cause a fundamental change in the enterprise, but it can bring commercial
success.
The relationship between DevOps and IT organizations
The IT organization is the carrier for enterprise-level DevOps practice. For enterprises, day-to-day
operations cannot proceed without the cooperation and support of IT organizations. Typically,
IT organizations are essential components for an enterprise’s sustainable operation, possessing
informatization and digitization attributes. In daily business activities, IT organizations are
required to have the following two core capabilities:
• Guided by the company’s strategic objectives, support enterprise strategy through
informatization and digitalization means
• Under the guidance of the overall informatization planning, build informatization and
digital infrastructure and application systems to provide technical support for enterprise
operations
The “entanglement” between IT organizations and DevOps originates from the IT organization’s
self-reform. In most enterprises, the pressures faced by IT organizations can be divided into
internal and external pressures. Internal pressure mainly comes from internal management
and coordination, while external pressure mainly arises from the service demands of business
departments. When external pressure needs to be relieved through internal management, the
innate capabilities of DevOps cannot cover all requirements. Today, more and more enterprises
are turning to DevOps. In addition to utilizing DevOps to improve efficiency and maintain high
standards and high-efficiency output, it is also necessary to ensure the rationality of external
pressure release. Some large internet companies, such as Netflix, Spotify, and Etsy, have achieved

52100.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52100.heading: Chapter 6 167
52100.content:
good results in this area in their practice.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 168
With scale and capability expansion, IT organizations develop from an “individual contributor
model” to a “multi-team coordination model,” leading to the division of responsibilities and the
connection of workflows—what we commonly refer to as IT organizational capability sub-domains,
such as project management, requirement management, product management, architecture
management, development management, testing management, operations management, and
security management within the delivery chain. In the delivery chain, capability sub-domains
exist as single nodes. While collaborating and connecting, there are goal conflicts beyond their
responsibilities.
Therefore, within IT organizations, DevOps must achieve seamless IT service processes and
resolve the contradictions among various capability sub-domains. This is an extension of DevOps’
innate capabilities. The focus here is on online collaboration across departments and teams,
and the delivery of information along the delivery pipeline through the DevOps philosophy. For
example, when deploying a system online using traditional methods, a lengthy explanation
document may be needed; whereas by using DevOps methods for system deployment, automated
deployment can be achieved through standard runtime environment selection, environment
setup, and orchestration of the deployment process. Additionally, such deployment methods
can be understood by operators, executed by machines, and the deployment process can also be
tracked and audited.
These examples show that DevOps is not only about improving collaboration between development
and operations. In larger IT organizations, it must also address the friction created by separate
capability domains, disconnected tools, and handoffs across the delivery pipeline. This makes
conflict resolution and delivery-chain integration the next steps in understanding DevOps at
enterprise scale.
Resolving conflicts and connecting the delivery chain
Resolving conflicts among capability sub-domains is the foundation; connecting application
lifecycle management and value delivery is the next step. For instance, from project initiation,
requirement collection, architecture design, code development, integration and build, code testing,
continuous deployment, code configuration, to go-live monitoring—the integration of toolsets,
followed by unified toolchains, and ultimately achieving the monetization of IT organizational
capabilities.

52101.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52101.heading: Chapter 6 169
52101.content:
Chapter 6 169
IT organizations need to achieve technology output and technology operations through DevOps
capabilities, with the following two characteristics:
• When IT organizations have business attributes, DevOps can create value
• Even when IT organizations do not have business attributes, DevOps can still contribute
value
After examining DevOps from the perspectives of enterprise value, IT organizations, and delivery-
chain integration, we can now define it more precisely. DevOps is not just a set of tools or a
simple merger of development and operations; it is a methodology for improving organizational
effectiveness, delivery quality, and value flow across the software lifecycle.
Defining DevOps as a delivery methodology
So what exactly is DevOps? On the surface, DevOps refers to the integration of development
and operations, which is also the native capability of DevOps—that is, using tools to help
developers perform some of the work of operations personnel, thereby reducing costs. However,
after we gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between DevOps, enterprises, and IT
organizations, we find that DevOps is actually a methodology —an organizational effectiveness
and quality management methodology. In the delivery pipeline capability subdomain, DevOps
removes barriers; in the project and requirements subdomain, DevOps enables precise process
control and risk management; in the software development and testing subdomain, DevOps
helps development and testing teams improve delivery efficiency while ensuring quality; in the
operations subdomain, DevOps enhances the efficiency of product releases and accelerates online
quality feedback.
Meanwhile, by using delivery pipeline tools to realize data collection and by managing the process
through metrics for feedback and optimization, organizational effectiveness and quality are
ultimately improved.
Once DevOps is understood as a methodology for improving organizational effectiveness and
delivery quality, the next step is to examine the capabilities that make this improvement possible
in practice. These capabilities include visualizing delivery data, shifting quality and security
activities earlier in the lifecycle, operating through data-driven feedback, improving collaboration,
and managing delivery-related risk.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 170
Digital visualization capabilities in DevOps
During the software delivery process, digital visualization possesses two capabilities: visualization
capability oriented toward the Terminal and visualization capability oriented toward the
environment. The ultimate effect depends on the final “destination” of software delivery, which
is what we often refer to as value.
Digital visualization terminal
As the most fundamental capability of IT organizations, many believe that the “terminal” target

52102.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52102.heading: Chapter 6 169
52102.content:
of digital visualization is the enterprise leadership. However, this is a misunderstanding. The
targets of digital visualization not only include the management and business operations levels
of the enterprise but also a large number of backend support organizations and all components
of the enterprise. This is key to the management of people, finance, and assets in the enterprise.
In addition to personnel, processes, resources, and decisions also need to leverage digital means
for data visualization support. For enterprises, the value of “people, finance, and assets” must
always serve the business. Therefore, the ultimate value of digital visualization lies in the service
value based on positive business feedback, which is similar to the measurement and indicator
systems of DevOps. Digital visualization provides decision support for the business and serves
as a basis for management improvement.
Digital visualization ultimately needs to return to the Terminal; here, the Terminal refers to the
object that promotes lean enterprise operations through digital visualization, including business
operations and IT operations. The Terminal uses the positive feedback capability of data to achieve
problem location and assist decision-making. Digital visualization presents the value of data,
while the Terminal needs to reflect and act based on the presented content.
In the actual process of data visualization, it is necessary to clarify the beneficiary, decision object,
metrics, and goals of data visualization.
Digital visualization scenarios
The Scenario of digital visualization is aimed at comprehensive digital enterprise management,
focusing on people, finance, and assets, with the business at the center. When planning a digital
visualization Scenario, it is necessary to specify the particular problem the Scenario can solve,
and, at the same time, ensure the Scenario can match the analytical conclusions and data paths.

52103.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52103.heading: Chapter 6 171
52103.content:
Chapter 6 171
Here is a simple example for illustration: before a product goes into operation, software is delivered
via DevOps. The speed and quality of software delivery directly affect the product’s post-launch
performance in the market. Thus, IT lean operation holds an important position in comprehensive
digital management. When IT is the core component of business, IT is direct productivity. When
IT is not a core business component, the value of IT is still to enable better enterprise operations;
therefore, IT lean operation and enterprise business value are interconnected. The best practice
DevOps metrics system covers enterprise cost management and evaluation management. Within
the resources and cost framework, it forms a deep scenario management capability for IT activities
and establishes a data-related information view, as shown in Figure 6.3.
Figure 6.3: DevOps scenario hierarchy
In the field of business operations, digital visualization needs to clearly identify the factors that
affect performance, commonly referred to as intelligent operations. Data is categorized by scenario,
usually including sales data, order data, user activity data, production capacity data, and product
data, and data performance is matched to evaluation metrics. For business operations, data
performance is a potential driving factor for business development trends; any data deviation may
affect whether the business progresses as planned. This form of visualization related to business
trends is referred to as a scenario in the digital visualization field. By analyzing data performance,
problems in business operations can be identified, and based on the driving factors, decision-
making can be assisted to make targeted adjustments and improvements.
Visualization gives teams the information they need to understand delivery performance and
business impact. The next capability is shift-left practice, where DevOps uses that information
earlier in the lifecycle to improve quality, security, and delivery outcomes before problems reach
production.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 172
DevOps technology shift-left capabilities
In the vast majority of enterprises, whether considered from the perspective of a profit center
or a cost center, the role of IT in business activities is increasingly moving forward. Especially
in scenarios where market demands change rapidly, delivering software that is “secure, stable,
efficient, and low-cost” enables enterprises to better respond to market fluctuations and deliver
business value. Therefore, technology infrastructure centered on DevOps has gradually become
the core of IT management in enterprise digital transformation and is also a focal point of practice
for traditional enterprises in the process of software delivery.

52104.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52104.heading: Chapter 6 171
52104.content:
New technology infrastructure
The new technological infrastructure of enterprises is represented by innovative technologies
such as DevOps, cloud computing, microservices, and artificial intelligence. At the objective
level, DevOps aligns IT organizations with business organizations, focusing on business value
and customer experience; at the cultural level, it promotes a high-trust cultural philosophy,
fostering seamless communication, and shared risk between IT, business, and other functional
organizations; at the technological empowerment level, it combines technology, and capabilities
to realize intelligent, agile, and digital platforms.
Best practices of DevOps in the IT field effectively achieve a shift-left for internal enterprise IT,
bringing products to market better and faster through cost efficiency, increased productivity,
and quality assurance, assisting business organizations in building systematic capabilities, and
increasing innovation and risk resistance of products through business innovation and exceptional
user experience.
The extent to which DevOps shifts left depends on IT’s influence in business operations as well
as the scope of its capability output. The role of DevOps in the process of enterprise digital
transformation is largely determined by the reshaping of IT leadership. IT leaders must have
forward-looking thinking and grasp strategies that drive digital transformation, providing
necessary IT services and products for enterprise digital transformation. Additionally, there is a
need to integrate IT resources, organizational structure, and technological innovation according
to enterprise strategic objectives, so that IT service capabilities are maximally oriented toward
business, creating the greatest value and achieving the goal of upgrading IT management in
digital transformation.

52105.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52105.heading: Chapter 6 173
52105.content:
Chapter 6 173
Application modernization
Application modernization is also an effective way to shift technology left. Application
modernization is a novel concept that leverages existing legacy applications to modernize the
underlying platform infrastructure, internal architecture, and functionality. Conceptually, it
is similar to low-code approaches. According to McKinsey Digital’s COVID recovery research,
enterprises with low digitalization levels suffered greater losses during the pandemic, while those
with a higher degree of digitalization were less impacted. The reason is that highly digitalized
companies, through DevOps practices, optimize process-driven and data-driven procedures to
enhance new technological infrastructure capabilities via value delivery. At the same time, they
facilitate application modernization practices, improving efficiency and multi-cloud portability
via modern infrastructure, thereby achieving compatibility between modern applications and
existing applications.
The essence of application modernization is to amend the traditional programming methods
of business applications, making them more closely aligned with the needs of business agility.
During the process of an application’s transition to modernization, the existing information
architecture, operation, and maintenance models, application development and testing processes,
business data management models, and security requirements all face significant challenges.
It’s like changing engines and motors during flight: enterprises must both ensure continuity
of business growth amidst current competition and guarantee the potential for revolutionary
business changes in the future.
Shift-left practices and application modernization help DevOps improve delivery before software
reaches production. However, DevOps must also support what happens after delivery: how
systems are monitored, how feedback is collected, how data is used, and how IT services continue
to support business outcomes. This is where the digital operations capability of DevOps becomes
important.
Strengthening digital operations with DevOps
In traditional concepts, DevOps technical operations mainly focus on scenarios for application
domain assurance and user experience, especially in areas such as user data feedback and
intelligent monitoring, establishing end-to-end data link channels between IT and business sides.
In the context of digital transformation, DevOps technical operations in the IT domain need to
extend and restructure data scenarios to realize the digital reconstruction of business applications.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 174
DevOps technical operations need to consume existing data, collect and inventory the entire data
system, establish and improve a data-driven system, and, while improving efficiency and quality,

52106.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52106.heading: Chapter 6 173
52106.content:
extend the ability to deliver data output to the entire IT process by taking a digital operations-
oriented approach. This helps enhance IT service capability, allowing IT organizations to provide
more effective services to customers in advance through a “data role.”
There are two approaches to DevOps technical operations within the IT domain: one is to achieve
business-defined technical operations, and the other is to achieve user-defined technical
operations.
Achieving business-defined technical operations
In the process of digital transformation, IT organizations need the capability to identify business
use cases, especially in the digital technology domain, and should keep up with trends in business
applications. For C-end business scenarios, more attention should be paid to the impact of digital
factors of “people” and “technology” on customer behavior in order to define business scenarios.
Therefore, DevOps capabilities should center around the definition of business scenarios, adapting
IT organizations and IT culture to achieve better, faster, and more effective business support. At
the same time, in the DevOps value delivery pipeline, IT organizational capabilities should focus
on business scenarios, using requirement shift-left and testing shift-left practices to analyze
the value and impact of the delivery process on business use cases and promptly optimize the
supporting capabilities of the IT organization.
Business-defined technical operations represent the top-level design for technological digital
transformation within IT organizations under DevOps, used to realize the rapid launch of
enterprise-strategic products.
Implementing user-defined technology operations
User definition requires focusing more on user scenarios, aligning value output with the IT
organizational architecture in terms of user experience, especially in customer-facing TOC (To
Customer) scenarios. User-defined technology operations empower infrastructure and application
architecture through DevOps, adapting to more flexible user interaction modes, enhancing user
stickiness, obtaining the fastest feedback from the user side, and achieving lifecycle management
of user behavior through user data analysis. This continuously optimizes the IT system’s service
capabilities, as shown in Figure 6.4.

52107.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52107.heading: Chapter 6 175
52107.content:
Chapter 6 175
Figure 6.4: DevOps empowerment methods
In terms of infrastructure, represented by DevOps integrated cloud management platforms, user
scenarios and resource output are formed into a closed loop, supporting the overall business
operation from a technical perspective. This ensures that business development and infrastructure
remain aligned, and IT costs can be allocated to business operations, thus reducing costs from
a business perspective.
In terms of application architecture, represented by DevOps integrated microservices architectures,
the service-oriented business model integration architecture is transformed into a unified agile
architecture. By means of microservices, user-defined scenarios are broken down into smaller
unit services. Through flexible inter-service interaction and collaboration, business changes can
be rapidly supported, enhancing the product’s ability to respond to high-frequency changes in
user interaction.
These business-defined and user-defined operations capabilities depend on more than data and
technical platforms. They also require teams to collaborate flexibly across departments, processes,
and tools as business needs change. This collaborative flexibility is another important DevOps
capability.
Enabling elastic collaboration through DevOps
DevOps’ elastic collaboration model is based on DevOps culture, breaking down communication
and collaboration barriers horizontally across departments and integrating people, processes, and
technology vertically, ultimately achieving continuous organizational improvement.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 176
DevOps introduces the cultural thinking of “value delivery” and “digital operations.” On the IT
side, digital value is extended, forming a closed loop in responding to market changes and feedback
through product delivery. This ultimately drives enterprises to reduce costs and increase efficiency
across a series of business stages, including market demand, product demand, product marketing,
and market feedback, achieving the desired goals. Under this collaboration model, the scope of
elasticity is related to how business changes occur. As the best accelerator for modern business
transformation, DevOps makes it easier for enterprises to adopt and rapidly realize business
ideas during digital transformation.
At the same time, in terms of personnel, process, and technology, DevOps continually and rapidly
delivers new value to customers through a more scientific collaboration approach, making
products better adapt to the ever-changing market and conveying the organization’s digital
profile to customers. When people, processes, and technology are aligned with the same business
goals, the digital transformation process becomes orderly and stable. Additionally, DevOps, via

52108.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52108.heading: Chapter 6 175
52108.content:
data-driven methods, carries out IT-side technical operations surrounding “people, finance, and
material” to achieve end-to-end delivery of resources, products, and value. This enables unified
resource planning and cost review, providing flexible collaboration for IT organizations regarding
task prioritization and resource scheduling.
DevOps’ role in digital transformation helps IT organizations improve efficiency, enhance
competitive posture, and increase participation in production activities, aiding the shift from
traditional hierarchical, command-and-control enterprises to digital organizations.
Business going online
A Business going online is a key milestone in software delivery. The type of enterprise, digital
scenarios, and transformation goals are always anchored to business value and company
operations, ultimately culminating in a business going online. On the IT side, this is usually
measured by “business continuity” indicators. For enterprises, the transition from offline to
online and the availability assurance of core systems are essential. For IT organizations, faster
and better product delivery, as well as more stable and higher-quality product maintenance, all
fall within the realm of business online.
Data-driven
The transformation of internal and external management and operation models in enterprises
through data-driven approaches usually involves two methods: First, evolving from process-
driven to data-driven, ensuring process compliance while improving the scientific nature of
execution and decision-making through data feedback; second, using data collaboration to mine
better business logic and organizational management models.

52109.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52109.heading: Chapter 6 177
52109.content:
Chapter 6 177
This is particularly evident in digital marketing and digital office fields, where shifts in user
relationships can be detected sensitively, and more scientific, compliant, and agile workflows
and standards can be built using labeling methods.
While data-driven collaboration improves visibility and decision-making, it also exposes new
risks. If delivery, testing, security, and user-experience data are incomplete or delayed, DevOps
teams may make decisions without enough evidence. For this reason, digital risk management
becomes an important part of mature DevOps practice.
Digital risk capabilities in DevOps
By analyzing best practice cases in DevOps, the author believes that digital risk is not limited only
to the measurement and feedback phase. The lack of advanced scenario-based testing data, end-to-
end security data, and the universality of user experience prediction are all manifestations of digital
risk. Common digital risk scenarios mainly include effectiveness evaluation of IT organizations,
post-evaluation and cost review of IT projects, and feedback and assurance in product operations.
Due to the characteristics of the DevOps culture, the collaborative environment and shared
responsibility model among IT members transmit product issues, which are ultimately reflected
in business scenarios through product operations. This is both an advantage of DevOps and a
potential risk factor in practice.
Lack of advanced scenario-based testing data
Testing is a critical link in the DevOps capability subdomain, responsible for the acceptance of
“product-level” deliverables—especially in the shift-left testing phase, where quality extends
to business requirements. Therefore, testing is essential for verifying whether applications or
services behave as expected and whether products can be delivered safely.
A lack of advanced scenario-based testing data often results in issues with stability and accuracy
in testing outcomes during value delivery, thus impacting product quality and safety. For digital-
assisted decision-making, complete testing data can simulate data changes and user conversion
journeys in business operations in advance. These advanced scenarios are oriented toward business
and requirements organizations while providing predictive positive feedback to digital users.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 178
End-to-end security data
By embedding security data into the DevOps “value delivery” chain through risk mitigation, risks
in the product delivery process can be effectively avoided, thereby amplifying the advantages of
DevOps. End-to-end security data allows for continuous monitoring of data performance during
software delivery and product operation. Through comprehensive visibility into service delivery
infrastructure, applications, their interdependencies, and intelligent business data analytics,

52110.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52110.heading: Chapter 6 177
52110.content:
it is possible to address potential threats before they impact business operations. At the same
time, the end-to-end security data covers all nodes in the product operation process, delivering
intelligence, and public opinion feedback in business language from the business perspective,
promoting digital visibility, and secure telemetry in digital operations.
Universality prediction of user experience
Traditional DevOps practices tend to focus more on requirements fulfillment and delivery cycles.
With the continuous evolution of user habits, the aggregation effect between DevOps and business
organizations is increasingly prominent, particularly in terms of the universality prediction of
user experience. According to authoritative statistics, user experience mainly centers on high
expectations of functionality and low tolerance for issues. Therefore, DevOps requires preemptive
digital feedback, covering user experience scenarios. From the user’s perspective, digital scenarios
should be extended to business planning, product requirements, testing data, release strategies,
and final business monitoring, enabling a comprehensive understanding of the business and
focusing on user experience, bringing in, and managing the visibility of the user experience
through digital visualization.
As DevOps practices mature, the same principles of automation, monitoring, feedback, and
lifecycle management are being extended to AI systems. This shift has led to related practices
such as MLOps and LLMOps, which adapt DevOps thinking to the development, deployment,
monitoring, and governance of machine learning and LLM applications.
DevOps in the era of LLMs
With the development of artificial intelligence technologies, more innovative technologies have
been introduced into the Ops field. Currently, there are two main directions: machine learning
and LLMs, which have ultimately led to MLOps (Machine Learning Operations) and LLMOps.
This chapter focuses on MLOps as a discipline — how the model-development work -
flow integrates with DevOps practice. The model-training techniques themselves
were covered in Chapter 4 (fine-tuning) and Chapter 5 (RAG and multi-agent systems).

52111.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52111.heading: Chapter 6 179
52111.content:
Chapter 6 179
The origin of MLOps
MLOps is a concept evolved from DevOps, referring to the application of DevOps ideas and
methods to the development, deployment, and operation and maintenance of machine learning,
aiming to improve the productivity and quality of machine learning models.
The concept of MLOps originated from the challenges enterprises faced when applying machine
learning in practice, mainly involving issues such as model deployment, operation and maintenance,
and monitoring. In traditional software development, a mature DevOps process has already been
established, and MLOps borrows from DevOps experience and thinking within the field of machine
learning to provide systematic and standardized solutions for machine learning development.
The MLOps process includes multiple stages such as data preparation, model selection, model
training, model deployment, model validation, and model updating, as shown in Figure 6.5.
Figure 6.5: Sequence of MLOps processes
Once the origin of MLOps is clear, the next question is how it changes the responsibilities of
DevOps teams in practice. MLOps keeps the core DevOps focus on automation, monitoring, and
continuous improvement, but extends it to the additional lifecycle needs of machine learning
systems.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 180
The role of MLOps
In practical application, based on the characteristics of machine learning, the role of MLOps—
beyond the traditional capabilities of DevOps—has added some specific scenarios, such as
redefining scenarios via model application, data collection, and organization, model training
and deployment, as well as continuous monitoring and updating. Nevertheless, the iteration, and
updating of technology are all aimed at improving the efficiency of software delivery.
Since MLOps originates from DevOps, the core philosophies of both are the same, covering
the initial tool-oriented and automated stages of construction, and sharing common paths for
optimization and feedback during adoption. However, there are also some differences: due to
differences in tech stacks, the trigger targets and methods differ. The trigger method for DevOps is
mainly code modification, while MLOps triggers are not limited to code changes—changes in data
or a decline in model performance (model degradation) can also trigger the pipeline. In addition,
MLOps includes additional steps necessary for building and training machine learning models,
such as data- and model-specific procedures, which means that there are subtle differences in
each component of the MLOps workflow.
In addition, in terms of workflow management, DevOps focuses on pipeline construction, while
MLOps emphasizes more on the management and automation of machine learning workflows,
as well as model deployment and monitoring.

52112.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52112.heading: Chapter 6 179
52112.content:
MLOps workflow based on DevOps
As shown in Figure 6.6, a standard MLOps workflow involves three roles: data engineer, model
engineer, and DevOps engineer.
Figure 6.6: Standard MLOps workflow

52113.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52113.heading: Chapter 6 181
52113.content:
Chapter 6 181
Data engineers are responsible for data annotation and ensuring data reliability and traceability;
model engineers are responsible for model management and ensuring model reproducibility
and iterability; DevOps engineers are responsible for application deployment and monitoring.
1. The main work in the data stage includes data collection, preprocessing, and feature
engineering:
• Data collection and preprocessing: This component is responsible for collecting
data from various sources (such as databases, file systems, APIs, etc.) and
performing preprocessing and cleaning, making the data suitable for training
and inference with machine learning models.
• Feature engineering: This component is responsible for transforming raw data
into features usable by machine learning models, including steps such as feature
selection, feature transformation, and feature construction.
2. The main tasks in the model stage include model training, model deployment, and model
monitoring and management:
• Model training: This component is responsible for training models using the
training data, including algorithm selection, model parameter tuning, and model
performance evaluation.
• Model deployment: This component is responsible for deploying trained models
to the production environment for real-time inference and prediction. It may
include steps such as packaging the model as an executable file, configuring the
model server, and monitoring model performance.
• Model monitoring and management: This component is responsible for
monitoring the performance and operating status of deployed models and making
adjustments and updates as needed. It may include monitoring metrics such as
model prediction accuracy, processing time, and resource usage.
3. The main work in the deployment stage is software release:
Although model output is uncertain and difficult to reproduce, the process of deploying
machine learning software to the production environment is reliable and repeatable and
aims to be as automated as possible.
MLOps provides a useful foundation for managing machine learning systems, but LLM-powered
applications introduce additional challenges, including prompt management, retrieval pipelines,
evaluation, model behavior monitoring, cost control, and governance. These differences have led
to the emergence of LLMOps.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 182
The origin of LLMOps
LLMOps is a set of tools and best practices for managing the lifecycle of LLM-powered applications.
It can be seen as a subcategory of MLOps, but there are certain differences between the two. These
differences stem from the different ways of building AI products with classic ML models versus
LLMs, primarily impacting data management, experimentation, evaluation, and cost.
DevOps improves software delivery by strengthening collaboration, automation, visibility,

52114.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52114.heading: Chapter 6 181
52114.content:
feedback, and lifecycle management. However, as organizations scale, teams often need a
more structured way to access the tools, environments, workflows, and infrastructure required
for delivery. This is where platform engineering becomes important: it turns shared delivery
capabilities into reusable internal platforms that reduce cognitive load and help teams deliver
software more consistently.
Building internal platforms for software delivery
Platform engineering extends DevOps practices by turning shared tools, infrastructure, workflows,
and knowledge into reusable internal platforms. Its goal is to reduce cognitive load for delivery
teams, improve developer experience, and make software delivery more consistent, secure, and
scalable.
The concept of platform engineering
Gartner describes platform engineering as gathering tools, capabilities, and processes—all
meticulously selected and packaged by domain experts—into a platform for end users. The
ultimate goal is to create a frictionless self-service experience, providing users with adequate
capabilities to complete critical tasks at minimal cost, thus increasing end-user productivity and
reducing cognitive load. The platform should meet all the needs of user teams and seamlessly fit
their preferred workflows in any possible form.
In the software delivery process, platform engineering aims to improve the efficiency and
effectiveness of software delivery teams, enabling enterprises to gain greater competitive
advantages in the market. By building a suite of tool platforms, software delivery teams can
deliver software application systems more efficiently and continuously, while ensuring their stable
operation. The core goal of platform engineering is to help software delivery teams enhance the
business value of the software they deliver.

52115.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
52115.heading: Chapter 6 183
52115.content:
Chapter 6 183
Within the software delivery system, platform engineering addresses how technical teams can
meet business needs at lower cost and with higher efficiency, while also solving various issues
in efficient business operations and enterprise digital transformation. Therefore, the value of
platform engineering lies in the infrastructure capabilities it provides, as well as the technical
services of the corresponding tool clusters. By using tool platforms to consolidate knowledge,
software delivery teams can improve overall efficiency and innovation.
The value of platform engineering in the software delivery process is reflected in the following
aspects:
• Reusability: Platform engineering has the capability for modular assembly. The technical
components and services provided by platform engineering can be shared and reused
across multiple applications, thus avoiding repetitive development and maintenance of
similar functions.
• Centralized Capability: Platform engineering possesses the ability to centrally manage
and monitor tools across domains. Users can more easily manage software applications
and the delivery process through tools, and use tools to maintain the entire application
lifecycle, thereby increasing the efficiency of software delivery and ensuring its stability.
• Scalability: Platform engineering integrates cloud-native capabilities, allowing the
elastically scalable cloud-native infrastructure to expand and upgrade smoothly and
quickly according to customer needs, in order to meet constantly changing business
requirements.
• Security: Platform engineering possesses security features, allowing software delivery
personnel to protect the security of applications and customer data through authentication,
authorization, and security services provided by platform engineering, thereby reducing
security risks.
After defining platform engineering and explaining its value in software delivery, the next step is
